cpp-api/CsvAccumulator.html.title: Concept CsvAccumulator | ExcelReader
cpp-api/CsvAccumulator.html.summary: Concept CsvAccumulator A fold over CSV records. Acc must be move-constructible; the wrapper returns the surviving accumulator by moving out of it. combine must fold next into *this without destroying it - the library owns next's lifetime and frees it afterwards. accumulate runs concurrently on worker threads, one Acc per partition, never on the calling thread. combine is effectively single-threaded but is not pinned to any particular thread and also never runs on the calling thread. ~Acc() does run on the calling thread, once the run has finished, and must not throw - std::move_constructible subsumes std::destructible, which is is_nothrow_destructible_v, so a throwing destructor fails this concept rather than reaching the shims. cpp-api/OpenOptions.html.summary: Struct OpenOptions Format, reader limits and CSV dialect for Workbook::open and aggregate_csv. A field left at 0 or XL_OPT_DEFAULT keeps the library default; on/off fields take XL_OPT_TRUE or XL_OPT_FALSE. An out-of-range value fails the open with XL_INVALID_ARGUMENT. struct xl::OpenOptions Fields Name Type Default Description format int32_t XL_FORMAT_AUTO An XL_FORMAT_* constant. XL_FORMAT_AUTO detects XLSX, XLSB and XLS from the signature; CSV has none and needs XL_FORMAT_CSV, except through an InputStream, where AUTO reads anything else as CSV. csv_sniff_dialect int32_t XL_OPT_DEFAULT Infer delimiter and quote from the start of a CSV. Off by default. csv_delimiter int32_t 0 CSV field separator byte. Default ,. csv_quote int32_t 0 CSV quote byte. Default ". csv_detect_bom int32_t XL_OPT_DEFAULT Skip a leading UTF-8 byte-order mark. On by default. max_total_decompressed_bytes int64_t 0 Bytes an XLSX/XLSB may inflate to, or an XLS workbook stream may declare. Default 512 MiB. max_cell_bytes int32_t 0 Largest cell value or buffered CSV record. Default 32 MiB. max_shared_string_bytes int64_t 0 Largest shared-string table. Default 128 MiB. max_zip_entries int32_t 0 Most entries an XLSX/XLSB archive may hold. Default 65,536. prefetch_decompression int32_t XL_OPT_DEFAULT Inflate XLSX/XLSB sheet data on a background thread ahead of parsing. Off by default. intern_strings int32_t XL_OPT_DEFAULT Deduplicate repeated text outside the shared-string table. Off by default; pays off only for low-cardinality text. source_cache_bytes int64_t 0 Block cache of a Source. Default 64 MiB. max_buffered_bytes int64_t 0 Most bytes an InputStream may supply before an XLSX, XLSB or XLS opens. source_block_size int32_t 0 Block size of a Source's cache. Default 4 MiB; negative turns the cache off. verify_zip_checksums int32_t XL_OPT_DEFAULT Check each XLSX/XLSB ZIP entry against its CRC-32. On by default; a mismatch fails the read. password std::string {} UTF-8 password that unlocks an encrypted OOXML workbook (.xlsx/.xlsb/.xlsm); empty for none. Open the workbook with XL_FORMAT_AUTO: XL_FORMAT_XLSX reads the encrypted container as a plain ZIP and fails before the password is checked.

cpp/README.html.title: excelreader (C++) | ExcelReader
cpp/README.html.summary: excelreader (C++) Header-only C++23 wrapper around ExcelReader's native C ABI: opening a workbook (from a path, memory, a random-access xl::Source or an xl::InputStream, with the full open-options surface), sheet navigation, schema inference, schema-driven typed table parsing, schema-driven writing, row-by-row decoded reads, and Arrow export. Requirements CMake 3.16+, a C++23 compiler (std::expected). Git symlink support: this package's include/xl is a symlink into src/ExcelReader.Native/include at the repo root. On Windows, either enable Developer Mode (Windows 10 1703+) or clone with git -c core.symlinks=true clone ... from an elevated shell — otherwise the symlink checks out as a plain text file containing the target path, and the build fails with "excelreader.h not found". Usage include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare(excelreader GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/GabrielMarquezMatte/ExcelReader.git GIT_TAG v7.0.0 SOURCE_SUBDIR cpp) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(excelreader) target_link_libraries(your_app PRIVATE xl::excelreader) excelreader_copy_native_library(your_app) FetchContent_MakeAvailable downloads the matching native binary for your platform from that tag's GitHub Release automatically (see cmake/FetchNativeLib.cmake). excelreader_copy_native_library puts that binary next to your executable once it links. On Windows it is required: the DLL is loaded by name at startup, and one that sits neither beside the executable nor on PATH makes the process exit with 0xc0000135 (STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND) before main runs. The call is a no-op elsewhere, where the rpath baked in at link time already resolves the library. Install once, find_package after Building cpp as its own project installs the headers, the native binary and a config package, so downstream projects find it without re-downloading anything: cmake -S cpp -B build/cpp -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --install build/cpp --config Release --prefix /your/prefix find_package(excelreader 7.0 REQUIRED) target_link_libraries(your_app PRIVATE xl::excelreader) Point CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH at the prefix you installed into. The native binary is resolved once, at install time — find_package never touches the network. The package version comes from EXCELREADER_VERSION, so a checkout that isn't on a tag installs as 0.0.0 and any versioned find_package request against it fails; pass -DEXCELREADER_VERSION=v7.0.0 to install under a real version. On Windows the generated import library is installed next to the DLL, and the package ships excelreader_copy_native_library as well, so a find_package consumer copies the DLL next to its executable the same way a FetchContent one does. Pass -DEXCELREADER_INSTALL=OFF to skip the install rules. They default off when cpp is pulled in with add_subdirectory/FetchContent, so a parent project's install step never picks them up. Build notes Two variables control where FetchNativeLib.cmake gets the native binary and which release it downloads from: EXCELREADER_NATIVE_LIB (environment variable) — path to a locally-built ExcelReader.Native.{dll,so,dylib} (e.g. from dotnet publish src/ExcelReader.Native -r win-x64) to use instead of downloading a release asset. Useful for local development and for CI, which builds the native lib fresh per PR (see .github/workflows/cpp.yml) rather than depending on a tag already being released. EXCELREADER_VERSION (CMake cache variable) — the release tag whose assets to download when EXCELREADER_NATIVE_LIB isn't set. Auto-detected from git describe --tags --exact-match when left empty; falls back to v0.0.0 when the checkout isn't exactly on a tag (e.g. a normal development branch). Example #include <xl/excelreader.hpp> struct Row { std::string_view Name; double Value; }; template<> struct xl::ExcelMapper<Row> { static constexpr auto get_bindings() { return std::make_tuple( xl::make_field("Name", &Row::Name), xl::make_field("Value", &Row::Value)); } }; auto workbook = xl::Workbook::open("book.xlsx"); auto table = xl::parse<Row>(workbook->sheet(0)); for (const auto& row : *table) { /* ... */ } Sheets and schema inference for (xl::Sheet sheet : *workbook->sheets()) { std::println("{}", sheet.name().value()); } // Guess a schema from the header row plus a sample of the data, before committing to one. for (const auto& column : *workbook->sheet(1).infer_schema(1, 100)) { // column.name is nullopt when the column must be resolved by column.index instead. } // With no row type, parse the sheet through that schema. The columns are the xl::ColumnRef // write_columns takes, so the table writes back as it was read. auto schema = workbook->sheet(1).infer_schema(); auto table = xl::parse(workbook->sheet(1), *schema); for (const xl::ColumnRef& column : table->columns()) { /* column.type, column.values, ... */ } auto written = xl::write_columns("copy.xlsx", table->columns()); // Or a batch at a time: an xl::TableReader, whose batches are xl::Tables. auto reader = xl::parse_batches(workbook->sheet(1), *schema, {.batch_size = 10'000}); for (auto& batch : *reader) { if (!batch) { break; } /* batch->columns() */ } A column matched by index has no name, and writing needs every column named or none. The schema is a guess over a sample: a column inferred as XL_T_I64 that holds a fraction further down fails the read, unless the column is nullable. Every entry point returns std::expected<T, xl::Error> — this header throws nothing. A workbook hands out sheets. An xl::Sheet is the workbook handle and an index: it owns nothing, it is cheap to copy, and every read on it opens its own cursor. workbook->sheet(i) makes no native call; an index outside the workbook is reported by the first read on the returned sheet. auto workbook = xl::Workbook::open("report.xlsx"); if (!workbook) { /* workbook.error().message */ } auto sheets = workbook->sheets().value(); for (xl::Sheet sheet : sheets) { std::println("{} {}", sheet.index(), sheet.name().value()); } if (auto totals = workbook->sheet_by_name("Totals").value()) { auto cursor = totals->rows().value(); while (auto row = cursor.next_row()) { // ... } } One open workbook can be read from several threads, which loads the shared-string table once: std::vector<std::thread> threads; for (xl::Sheet sheet : sheets) { threads.emplace_back([sheet] { auto table = xl::parse<Row>(sheet); /* ... */ }); } for (std::thread &thread : threads) { thread.join(); } A cursor, a typed reader and an Arrow stream are each used by one thread at a time, and keep working after the workbook is destroyed. A Sheet does not: take what you need from it first. Tables tables() lists the workbook's Excel tables ("Format as Table" ranges) as xl::TableInfo: name, the sheet holding it, and its 0-based range, header and totals rows included. table(index) and table_by_name(name) (ignoring case) return an xl::Sheet bounded to the table, so every read works on it and starts at the table's header row: for (const xl::TableInfo &table : *workbook->tables()) { std::println("{} on sheet {}: rows {}..{}", table.name, table.sheet, table.first_row, table.last_row); } if (auto sales = workbook->table_by_name("Sales").value()) { auto rows = xl::parse<Row>(*sales); } Cells keep the column indexes of the sheet holding the table, and the table's name() is that sheet's. A table is read on one thread whatever the degree of parallelism asks for. Reading rows one at a time Sheet::rows() returns a cursor over that sheet. Each row borrows a buffer the cursor reuses, so iterating allocates nothing per row. A clean end of sheet arrives as an error carrying XL_EOF: auto workbook = xl::Workbook::open("book.xlsx").value(); auto cursor = workbook.sheet(0).rows().value(); while (auto row = cursor.next_row()) { for (auto cell : *row) { std::print("{}\t", cell.value); } std::println(); } Each row is invalidated by the next next_row(). To hold every row at once, use Sheet::read_all(), which decodes the whole sheet in one native call and owns it until destroyed: auto rows = workbook.sheet(0).read_all().value(); for (auto row : rows) { std::println("{} cells", row.size()); } xl::parse<T> remains the fastest way to read a sheet whose columns you know. Chunked reads For a sheet too large to hold in memory at once, xl::parse_batches<T> is xl::parse<T> delivered a batch at a time: auto workbook = xl::Workbook::open("book.xlsx").value(); auto reader = xl::parse_batches<Row>(workbook.sheet(0), {.batch_size = 10'000}).value(); for (auto &batch : reader) { if (!batch) { break; } for (const auto &row : *batch) { /* ... */ } } parse_batches returns std::expected<xl::TypedReader<T>, xl::Error>; next() returns std::expected<std::optional<TableView<T>>, Error>, an empty optional at end of sheet, and TypedReader is also an input range, so the range-for above works directly. batch_size is rows per batch and must be positive (0 or negative is XL_INVALID_ARGUMENT; read a whole sheet with parse). Each batch is independent and outlives the reader. Several typed readers and Arrow streams may be open on one workbook at once; each read is independent. Encrypted workbooks OpenOptions::password unlocks a password-protected OOXML workbook (.xlsx/.xlsb/.xlsm) through any Workbook::open overload: auto workbook = xl::Workbook::open("protected.xlsx", {.password = "hunter2"}); if (!workbook) { if (workbook.error().code == XL_STATUS_PASSWORD_REQUIRED) { /* no password was supplied */ } else if (workbook.error().code == XL_STATUS_PASSWORD_INCORRECT) { /* ask again */ } else { /* workbook.error().message - unsupported scheme or a corrupt file; not worth retrying */ } } Unlike the Rust/Python bindings, this header never throws — XL_STATUS_PASSWORD_REQUIRED and XL_STATUS_PASSWORD_INCORRECT (from excelreader.h) are reported as ordinary xl::Error::code values on the std::unexpected returned from open, distinguishable from any other failure without parsing error().message. Writing an encrypted workbook is a second step: write the plaintext package with write_columns/ write_sheet, then wrap it with xl::encrypt_package, which produces an agile-encrypted (ECMA-376 4.4) CFB container — AES-256-CBC, SHA-512, 100,000 spin iterations, with a dataIntegrity HMAC: auto written = xl::write_columns("plain.xlsx", columns); auto encrypted = xl::encrypt_package("plain.xlsx", "secret.xlsx", "hunter2"); if (!encrypted) { /* encrypted.error().message */ } package_path is read twice (it is not disposed or removed), so it must already be a finished file. Encryption parameters are fixed at Excel's own defaults — there are no options — and only XLSX/XLSB packages can be encrypted, matching what Workbook::open can decrypt. Reading from your own bytes Derive from xl::Source to read from anything you can read at an offset; read_at is called from several threads, in cached 4 MiB blocks. Derive from xl::InputStream for a stream that cannot seek: a CSV is read as it arrives, an XLSX, XLSB or XLS is read whole first. class StdinStream final : public xl::InputStream { public: std::expected<std::size_t, std::string> read(std::span<std::byte> buffer) override { std::cin.read(reinterpret_cast<char *>(buffer.data()), static_cast<std::streamsize>(buffer.size())); if (std::cin.bad()) { return std::unexpected(std::string("reading stdin failed")); } return static_cast<std::size_t>(std::cin.gcount()); } }; auto workbook = xl::Workbook::open(std::make_unique<StdinStream>(), {.format = XL_FORMAT_CSV}); The workbook owns the object you pass and deletes it once nothing needs it. A returned error string or a thrown exception becomes the xl::Error of the call that needed the bytes. Arrow export <xl/excelreader_arrow.hpp> is a separate header — including <xl/excelreader.hpp> never pulls the Arrow C Data Interface declarations in. It does not depend on the Apache Arrow C++ library: you get the raw ArrowArray/ArrowSchema pair, owned by an RAII xl::ArrowTable, to hand to whichever Arrow implementation you already link. #include <xl/excelreader_arrow.hpp> auto workbook = xl::Workbook::open("book.xlsx"); auto table = xl::to_arrow<Row>(workbook->sheet(0)); // table->array / table->schema are a top-level struct array; both release in ~ArrowTable. Batched: xl::to_arrow_stream<T> is xl::to_arrow<T> delivered a batch at a time. next() returns an xl::ArrowTable holding the batch and its own copy of the schema (schema() returns one whose array is empty); each releases exactly once and outlives the stream that produced it: auto stream = xl::to_arrow_stream<Row>(workbook->sheet(0), {.batch_size = 10'000}); while (true) { auto batch = stream->next(); if (!batch || !batch->has_value()) { break; } // (*batch)->array is this one batch } Same header_row/batch_size meaning as xl::parse_batches above. With no row type, both take the columns at run time instead, such as the ones infer_schema returned. A column with a name is matched by it, one without by its index: auto schema = workbook->sheet(0).infer_schema(); auto table = xl::to_arrow(workbook->sheet(0), *schema); auto stream = xl::to_arrow_stream(workbook->sheet(0), *schema, {.batch_size = 10'000}); The schema is a guess over a sample: a column inferred as XL_T_I64 that holds a fraction further down fails the read, unless the column is nullable. Writing Two layers, mirroring the two on the reading side. xl::write_sheet<T> uses the same xl::ExcelMapper<T> specialization xl::parse<T> reads with, so a round trip needs one mapping, not two: std::vector<Row> rows = /* ... */; auto written = xl::write_sheet("out.xlsx", rows); // format inferred from the extension if (!written) { std::fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", written.error().message.c_str()); } If you already hold columnar buffers, xl::write_columns hands them to the ABI with no copy — they are borrowed for the duration of the call and must outlive it: std::vector<int64_t> ids{1, 2, 3}; std::vector<double> values{0.5, 1.5, 2.5}; std::array<xl::ColumnRef, 2> columns{ xl::i64_column("id", ids), xl::f64_column("value", values)}; auto written = xl::write_columns("out.xlsx", columns); Both functions also write into memory: pass a std::vector<std::uint8_t>& instead of a path and it is replaced with the file's bytes. There is no extension to infer the format from, so name it: std::vector<std::uint8_t> bytes; auto written = xl::write_sheet(bytes, rows, {.format = XL_FORMAT_XLSX}); One constructor per column type: i64_column, f64_column, bool_column, date_column, time_column, timestamp_column, and string_column (which takes an int32 offsets span of rows + 1 entries plus the UTF-8 blob). A nullable column is a values buffer plus an LSB-first validity bitmap — bit set means the row is valid — passed as the last argument to any of those constructors. write_columns checks the bitmap is long enough for the row count before calling: the ABI takes it without a length and reads (rows + 7) / 8 bytes on trust, so a short one would be a buffer overrun. On the struct side, declare the field std::optional<T> and write_sheet builds the bitmap for you. xl::WriteOptions sets the format, the sheet name, the CSV dialect, and the XLS/XLSB and XLSX/XLSB toggles. Its format defaults to XL_FORMAT_AUTO, which takes the format from the path's extension (.xlsx, .xlsb, .xls or .csv, in any case); an unrecognized extension, or AUTO with a vector destination, fails the write rather than silently choosing a format. For XLSX and XLSB, degree_of_parallelism formats and compresses batches of batch_rows rows on several threads: 0 uses every processor, 1 (the default) writes serially, and batch_rows = 0 keeps the library default of 8,192. The columns must not change while the write runs. With use_shared_strings on, two parallel runs give the same content in files that differ byte for byte. XLS, CSV and xl::WriterHandle's per-cell writes ignore both fields. xl::write_columns("big.xlsx", columns, {.degree_of_parallelism = 0}); write_sheet walks the range once and appends each field to its own column buffer, with the per-field dispatch resolved at compile time. That transpose is the only copy it makes, and it is what the ABI's columnar shape costs a row-shaped caller; write_columns pays nothing. Writing cell by cell xl::WriterHandle writes a workbook as calls arrive, sheet by sheet, without holding it in memory first. Only finish() commits: destroying a handle that was not finished, an early return or an exception included, discards what was written and leaves an existing file at the path as it was, as abort() does. Opened over a std::vector<std::uint8_t>&, the handle fills the vector when it finishes. auto writer = xl::WriterHandle::open("out.xlsx").value(); writer.start_sheet("Totals"); writer.start_row(); writer.write(std::string_view("widgets")); writer.write(int64_t{7}); writer.write(std::optional<double>{}); // a blank cell writer.end_row(); writer.end_sheet(); if (auto done = writer.finish(); !done) { /* done.error().message */ } Every call returns std::expected<void, xl::Error>; one out of order fails instead of corrupting the file. To write several sheets from whole tables, call the handle's write_sheet or write_columns once per sheet. They take what the free functions take, plus the sheet's name, and write it in one call instead of one per cell, using the handle's degree_of_parallelism and batch_rows. Between sheets they mix with start_sheet..end_sheet; while a sheet is open they fail. auto writer = xl::WriterHandle::open("report.xlsx", {.degree_of_parallelism = 0}).value(); writer.write_sheet("Sales", sales); // a range of ExcelMapper rows writer.write_columns("Stock", columns); // xl::ColumnRefs, such as an xl::Table's if (auto done = writer.finish(); !done) { /* done.error().message */ } An xl::TableOptions as the last argument writes the sheet as an Excel table, with filter buttons and a table style (XLSX and XLSB only, every column named). The name must be unique in the workbook; the style defaults to TableStyleMedium2, and .style = std::nullopt leaves the table unstyled: writer.write_sheet("Sales", sales, xl::TableOptions{.name = "Sales", .style = "TableStyleLight9"}); Aggregating a CSV in parallel xl::aggregate_csv<Acc> folds a CSV file or buffer across worker threads. Each partition starts from a copy of the seed, accumulate sees each record, and combine merges partitions: struct RowCount { int64_t rows = 0; int32_t accumulate(xl::RowView) noexcept { ++rows; return XL_OK; } int32_t combine(RowCount &next) noexcept { rows += next.rows; return XL_OK; } }; auto counted = xl::aggregate_csv("big.csv", RowCount{}, {.csv_delimiter = ';'}, /*header_row*/ 1); The dialect (csv_delimiter, csv_quote, csv_detect_bom) and max_cell_bytes come from xl::OpenOptions; the header row and the degree of parallelism (0 = every processor) follow it. Callback reads Sheet::for_each_row calls a function once per row on the calling thread, with cells borrowed from the library's buffers for that call instead of copied into a cursor: double total = 0; auto walked = workbook->sheet(0).for_each_row([&](xl::RowView row) { if (row.size() > 1) { total += row[1].as_number().value_or(0); } return XL_OK; }); Sheet::aggregate folds any sheet, in any format, across worker threads; the accumulator has the same shape as for aggregate_csv, so RowCount above works unchanged. New code should use it rather than aggregate_csv: auto counted = workbook->sheet(0).aggregate(RowCount{}, /*header_row*/ 1); A cell in these callbacks carries text, a number, or both. value holds only the stored text, so it is empty for a cell that carries only a number; text() formats that number itself (shortest round-trip form) and as_number() returns it directly, or parses the text when there is no number. A return other than XL_OK stops the run and comes back as the error's code (use positive codes), and an exception is reported as an error. Calling other functions on the workbook from inside the callback is allowed. Sheet::aggregate seeds a copy per chunk of sheet data, not per thread, and may destroy a chunk's copy without combining it; XLS, table views and CSV opened from a Source or InputStream read sequentially. Bounds and ABI TableView::operator[] is unchecked, like std::vector's. Use TableView::at(row), which returns std::optional<T> and is nullopt outside [0, size()). Every entry point that starts native work (xl::Workbook::open, write_columns, write_sheet, WriterHandle::open, encrypt_package and aggregate_csv) first checks the loaded library's xl_abi_version() against the XL_ABI_VERSION this header was compiled against, and fails with an explanatory xl::Error rather than reading native memory through a layout that may have changed. xl::abi_version() exposes the loaded revision directly. Benchmarks Google Benchmark suite in benchmarks/, opt-in via -DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON. Measured on Windows 10 (22H2), 16 logical CPUs @ 3.39 GHz, MSVC 19.51 (Release), Google Benchmark v1.9.1, --benchmark_repetitions=10 (means shown). Benchmark RealExcel.xlsb (100 rows) 65K_Records_Data.xlsb (65,535 rows) open (from memory) 22.7 µs 1.23 ms parse (4 or 6 bound columns) 44.6 µs 23.8 ms parse_batches, batches of 1,000 / 10,000 rows - 22.6 ms / 23.1 ms infer_schema (sample 100 / 1,000 rows) 72.4 µs 607.0 µs open here is the byte-span overload, which copies the caller's buffer before returning (the caller may free it afterwards), so it scales with file size: 1.23 ms is mostly copying the 3.7 MB fixture. Opening by path reads only the package directory and stays nearly flat — see the Rust suite below. parse scales linearly with rows × columns, at roughly 360 ns/row here. Draining the same sheet through the batched typed reader costs the same as one whole-sheet parse while holding only one batch in memory at a time. infer_schema scales with its sample size, not the file's total row count. A separate opt-in suite (-DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS_COMPARE=ON, gated separately because it pulls in xlnt and xlsxio as heavy source builds — xlsxio's own dependencies, expat and minizip, are fetched and compiled directly against it) compares against both reading 65K_Records_Data.xlsx in full (all 14 columns, 65,535 rows; neither competitor reads .xlsb, so this comparison is xlsx-only). All three sides decode every cell into an owned value (std::string for text, not the zero-copy std::string_view used above) so none gets a zero-copy advantage the others can't take: Library Mean ExcelReader (parse<FullRow>) 58.0 ms DuckDB (read_xlsx, summing every column in SQL) 417.8 ms xlsxio (xlsxioread_sheet_next_cell_*) 515.5 ms xlnt (worksheet::rows() + cell::to_string()/value<double>()) 2,495.0 ms ExcelReader is ~7.2x faster than DuckDB, ~8.9x faster than xlsxio and ~43x faster than xlnt on this workload. xlsxio is a lean, purpose-built C streaming reader — the same abstraction level as ExcelReader's own native core — so it was the strongest of the two competitors tested, though still well behind. Run locally: cmake -S cpp -B build -DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build build --config Release --target excelreader_cpp_benchmarks ./build/benchmarks/excelreader_cpp_benchmarks --benchmark_repetitions=10 --benchmark_report_aggregates_only=true Add -DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS_COMPARE=ON -DCMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5 (xlnt's own CMakeLists.txt predates CMake's minimum-version floor) and build/run excelreader_cpp_compare_benchmarks for the xlnt/xlsxio comparison. CSV against zsv excelreader_cpp_csv_compare_benchmarks (-DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS_ZSV=ON) reads 65K_Records_Data.csv (8.2 MB, 65,535 rows × 14 columns, CRLF, UTF-8 BOM) against zsv v1.4.3, a SIMD CSV parser in C, with both of its engines: the default (compat) and the branchless SIMD one (fast, scan_engine = 3). zsv uses GCC vector extensions MSVC cannot compile, so this target needs GCC or Clang, and it is its own executable because the DuckDB comparison above only links under MSVC. Two workloads: Typed: parse<FullRow> against zsv plus the same conversions done by hand (std::string for text, ISO dates, std::from_chars for the integers and doubles), one owned FullRow per row. All three produce the same checksum. Cells: every cell's bytes counted. ExcelReader goes through RowCursor (xl_rows_next_view), zsv through its row handler. zsv's checksum is 3 bytes higher because it keeps the BOM in the first header cell. Measured on the same machine as above, GCC 16.2.0 (MSYS2 UCRT64, -O3 -mavx2 for zsv), Release, --benchmark_repetitions=10 (means shown): Workload ExcelReader zsv compat zsv fast Typed, 14 columns into FullRow 28.1 ms 24.0 ms 21.2 ms Cells, byte count 11.8 ms 5.8 ms 3.5 ms zsv is faster on both. Typed, it is ~1.2x (compat) and ~1.3x (fast) faster than ExcelReader. Counting cells, it is ~2.0x and ~3.4x faster. The cells gap is the C ABI, not the CSV parser. xl_rows_next_view copies every cell's value into a native row the cursor owns, one call per row, and that alone costs ~10.6 ms here (calling it without reading any cell, measured separately). The managed reader reads the same file in ~5 ms under BenchmarkDotNet (RealDataReadBenchmark.Csv_ExcelReader), but that is a different harness and runtime, so it is context rather than a like-for-like number. The ExcelReader rows were 34.2 ms (typed) and 14.3 ms (cells) before the NativeAOT library's static PGO profile was regenerated (a namespace refactor had left it matching none of the hot methods) and its x64 build was pinned to x86-64-v3. The cells row was 30.5 ms before that, when xl::RowView still decoded each cell through std::optional helpers. The rows are from separate 10-repetition runs (typed CVs 2–5%, cells CVs ≤1.3%). A first run had CVs up to 20% and was discarded. Run locally, on Windows from an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell with gcc and ninja: cmake -S cpp -B build-zsv -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_POLICY_DEFAULT_CMP0168=NEW \ -DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON -DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS_ZSV=ON cmake --build build-zsv --target excelreader_cpp_csv_compare_benchmarks ./build-zsv/benchmarks/excelreader_cpp_csv_compare_benchmarks --benchmark_repetitions=10 --benchmark_report_aggregates_only=true The MinGW Makefiles generator failed here inside FetchContent's sub-build. Configuring with Ninja and CMAKE_POLICY_DEFAULT_CMP0168=NEW worked. Under MinGW the executable links its runtime statically, so it does not pick up another toolchain's libstdc++-6.dll from PATH. Writing excelreader_cpp_write_benchmarks (same -DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON flag) measures the two write layers against each other over 7 columns of the same fixture. Both cases write the same columns, so the gap between them is only the cost of starting from row-shaped data: BM_WriteColumns is handed buffers that are already columnar, while BM_WriteSheet starts from a std::vector<Row> and pays the row-to-column transpose. Benchmark Time Rows/s BM_WriteColumns (pre-transposed) 34.0 ms 1.94 M/s BM_WriteSheet (from std::vector<Row>) 39.9 ms 1.64 M/s The transpose costs ~17% here. It is not free, but it is not the dominant cost of producing the file — see the comparison below, where the same two cases over 14 columns land within ~16–17%. excelreader_cpp_write_compare_benchmarks (under -DEXCELREADER_BUILD_BENCHMARKS_COMPARE=ON) puts that against xlnt, xlsxio and DuckDB's excel extension, all writing the full 14-column, 65,535-row shape of 65K_Records_Data.xlsx from the same in-memory rows. libxlsxwriter — same author as rust_xlsxwriter, and, like xlsxio, a streaming C writer with no document-model overhead — is measured separately, by excelreader_cpp_write_compare_lxw_benchmarks: xlsxio and libxlsxwriter each vendor their own incompatible copy of minizip and export the same C symbols (zipOpen, zipOpenNewFileInZip, ...), so linking both into one binary let calls cross between the two implementations and corrupted xlsxio's output — see Known issue below. Building both write-compare targets and running them back to back is required to see every competitor. Library Wall CPU ExcelReader (xl::write_columns, pre-transposed) 65.3–65.7 ms 65.3–66.8 ms ExcelReader (xl::write_sheet<FullRow>) 76.2–76.5 ms 76.4 ms DuckDB (COPY ... TO ... WITH (FORMAT xlsx)) 834.6–834.9 ms 828.1–843.8 ms libxlsxwriter (worksheet_write_string/_number) 1,200.4 ms 1,203.1 ms xlsxio (xlsxiowrite_add_cell_*) 2,441.4 ms 859.4 ms xlnt (worksheet::cell().value() + save()) 5,554.0 ms 5,546.9 ms Same machine as above; Google Benchmark's own iteration counts, no --benchmark_repetitions (each iteration writes a whole 65,535-row file, so the slower cases run once or a handful of times). xlnt and xlsxio only build into excelreader_cpp_write_compare_benchmarks; libxlsxwriter only into excelreader_cpp_write_compare_lxw_benchmarks (see the known issue below) — the ExcelReader and DuckDB rows appear in both, and the small ranges above are those two independent runs, not repeated sampling within one run. write_sheet — the matched-work number, since it starts from the same std::vector<FullRow> every competitor is handed — is ~11x faster than DuckDB, ~16x faster than libxlsxwriter, ~32x faster than xlsxio, and ~73x faster than xlnt on wall time. Known issue: xlsxio + libxlsxwriter cannot share a binary An earlier version of excelreader_cpp_write_compare_benchmarks linked xlnt, xlsxio, libxlsxwriter and DuckDB into one executable. xlsxio (built against minizip-ng's compat layer, whose zipOpenNewFileInZip takes uint16_t extrafield sizes) and libxlsxwriter (which vendors classic minizip, whose same-named function takes 32-bit uInt sizes and starts with if (size_extrafield_local > 0xffff) return ZIP_PARAMERROR; — a check that cannot exist in the minizip-ng version) both export identical C symbol names from a static library linked into that one binary. The linker kept exactly one definition of each name, so a call could resolve to the wrong implementation — a zipFile opened by one library's zipOpen got handed to the other library's zipOpenNewFileInZip, which read it through an incompatible struct layout. That is what produced Error creating file "xl/workbook.xml" inside zip file on xlsxio's background thread in Release builds (Debug's different link order happened not to trigger it) — and it was silent otherwise: xlsxiowrite_close() still returned success with the workbook.xml entry missing, so the benchmark published a timing for a file that was skipping work, not a valid xlsx. The fix is structural: xlsxio and libxlsxwriter now build into two separate executables (excelreader_cpp_write_compare_benchmarks and excelreader_cpp_write_compare_lxw_benchmarks, both compiled from benchmark_write_compare.cpp under an #ifdef) that are never linked together. Every case in both executables also reopens the file it just wrote, outside the timed loop, before trusting its own timing — a writer that silently drops a required part now fails the benchmark instead of publishing a number for a broken file. libxlsxwriter's number barely moved after the fix (1,188.0 ms wall vs. 1,226.9 ms pre-fix, ~3%, inside normal run-to-run noise) and its CPU stayed essentially equal to wall time both before and after — consistent with the corruption running through xlsxio's calls resolving into libxlsxwriter's minizip, not the reverse: libxlsxwriter's own output was apparently never affected. That is a plausible explanation for the asymmetry, not a second confirmed fact — the collision could in principle run either direction depending on link order, and this project isn't going to re-derive MSVC's exact symbol-resolution algorithm to be certain which way it went here. Caveats, none of them optional when quoting these: xlsxio's CPU time is not stable across runs. It read 843.8–906.3 ms before the fix (some runs missing the workbook.xml entry), 1,171.9 ms and 687.5 ms in the two runs after it, 1,015.6 ms and 843.8 ms in the next two, 953.1 ms in the one after, 1,125.0 ms in the next and 859.4 ms in the latest, while its wall time stayed at ~2.4 s throughout. Its wall time is dominated by I/O wait — CPU is well under half of wall, against every other case here being CPU-bound (wall ≈ CPU) — so quote the wall-time ratio, which is what a caller waits. Against this run's CPU time the gap from write_sheet to xlsxio is ~11x, not ~32x. ExcelReader does slightly more work here, not less: it attaches a number format to the two date columns so Excel shows a date, while every competitor case writes those as bare serial numbers. That difference favours the competitors. xlnt builds a full document model (styles, formats, formulas) before serializing, which is more than this library exposes at all. Its number reflects a different feature set, not only a slower path. DuckDB's rows are loaded via its Appender API before the timed region, so its number measures COPY ... TO ... xlsx alone — the same treatment write_columns gets for its transpose. DuckDB is a full analytical query engine doing far more than any Excel-writing library here; this measures one narrow slice of it, not "DuckDB" as a whole. The two ExcelReader cases land within ~16–17% of each other. The transpose's share grew as producing the file got cheaper, but it is still a minority of the cost. Reach for write_columns when your data is already columnar, but write_sheet is not the slow path.

docs/README.html.title: docs | ExcelReader
docs/README.html.summary: docs Evidence behind decisions in this codebase: benchmark results, memory-footprint measurements, approaches that were prototyped and rejected, and the reasoning that picked one design over another. STYLEGUIDE.md keeps this content out of the source. A comment asserting // 2.4x faster cannot be checked, cannot be re-run, and is wrong the moment anything around it changes. A document with the numbers, the machine and the corpus can be reproduced and argued with. What belongs here A measurement that justified a constant, a buffer size, a cache, or a data structure. A design that was tried and abandoned, with the numbers that killed it. These are the most valuable documents here — they are what stops the same idea being rebuilt next year. A performance ceiling and what it is bounded by. Usage documentation under guide/, split out of the root README so the NuGet landing page stays short. This is prose for a caller deciding how to use the library, not a substitute for the /// comments that document what each member does. What does not Plans, specs and task breakdowns. Those are working artifacts with a short life; they do not get committed, and the style guide forbids pointing a comment at one. Reference documentation of the public surface. That is /// XML doc comments, shipped in the package — never duplicated in guide/, which would then drift. Anything the code itself should be saying through naming and flow. Writing one State the machine, the corpus and the tool, so the numbers can be reproduced and disagreed with. Record what was measured, not only what was concluded — including the runs that came out flat or negative. Say explicitly what was not measured; an untested assumption presented as a result is the one failure mode that makes a document worse than no document. Where a finding constrains the code, the code may state the constraint on its own terms (a cap, an invariant) without restating the evidence for it. Index performance/reader-performance.md — where read time goes in each format, the ceiling on each, and the optimizations measured and rejected. performance/benchmarks.md — throughput and allocation against Sep, Sylvan, OfficeIMO and SpreadCheetah. guide/ — usage documentation: reading, parsing, writing, csv, encryption, errors, untrusted input.

docs/guide/csv.html.title: CSV | ExcelReader
docs/guide/csv.html.summary: CSV Reading, dialect sniffing and writing delimited text. Parallel CSV parsing is covered in reading.md. Read CSV CsvReader is a workbook with exactly one, unnamed sheet (csv.FirstSheet, the same sheet as csv.Sheets[0]). It streams RFC 4180 CSV (quoted fields, embedded delimiters/newlines, ""-escaped quotes) through the same Row/Cell model as the Excel workbooks, so ExcelParser<T> works on it unchanged. using ExcelReader.Core.Parser; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; using var csv = Excel.FromCsvFile("report.csv"); foreach (var row in csv.FirstSheet) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } // Typed parsing works exactly like the Excel workbooks: foreach (var item in ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ChangeRow>().Parse(csv.FirstSheet)) { Console.WriteLine($"{item.File}: +{item.LinesAdded}"); } Excel.FromCsv/FromCsvFile/FromCsvAsync/FromCsvFileAsync mirror the other formats' factory shape and take the same ExcelReaderOptions. Its Csv property, a CsvReaderOptions, changes the delimiter/quote character, supplies a non-UTF-8 Encoding (transcoded to UTF-8 internally), or turns off BOM detection; MaxCellBytes and InternStrings stay on ExcelReaderOptions, as for every format: var options = new ExcelReaderOptions { Csv = new CsvReaderOptions { Delimiter = (byte)';' } }; using var csv = Excel.FromCsvFile("relatorio.csv", options); Every CSV cell is text (CellType.ExcelString, or CellType.Empty for a blank field); at the reader level there is no binary numeric or date representation, so Cell.TryGetDateTime/IsDate1904 (always false for CSV) do not apply. The typed parser, however, is CSV-specialized: ExcelParser<T>.Parse(CsvSheet) parses DateTime/DateOnly columns directly from the cell text (ISO or culture format, honoring Culture — e.g. pt-BR 02/07/2026), so no [ExcelConverter] is needed for dates. All the usual attributes work unchanged ([ExcelColumn] aliases, [ExcelRequired], [ExcelConverter]), and a converter still takes precedence over the built-in date parsing. (Holding the sheet as an IExcelSheet instead routes through the generic Excel pipeline, where dates use serial-number semantics — prefer the concrete Parse(CsvSheet) overload for CSV.) A CsvReader over memory, a file path or a seekable stream allows several enumerators at once, each reading the sheet from the start. Over a seekable stream, every enumerator starts at the position the stream had when the CsvReader was created; where the stream's position ends up afterwards is unspecified, so do not rely on it (a file stream, and a memory stream with an exposed buffer, are read without touching it). A non-seekable stream can be read once: a second enumeration throws InvalidOperationException. Excel.Open/OpenAsync do not auto-detect CSV — plain text has no magic-byte signature to sniff. Name the format instead: every Open/OpenAsync overload takes an optional ExcelFileFormat, and ExcelReaderOptions.Csv carries the dialect, so a caller that decides the format from an extension or a content-type header configures both families through one options object: ExcelFileFormat format = Path.GetExtension(path) is ".csv" ? ExcelFileFormat.Csv : ExcelFileFormat.Unknown; using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open(path, format, new ExcelReaderOptions { Password = secret, // used by the Excel formats Csv = CsvReaderOptions.Default with { SniffDialect = true }, // used by the CSV format }); ExcelFileFormat.Unknown keeps the signature-based detection the no-format overloads do; EncryptedOoxml is a detection result rather than something to open, so passing it throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Sniff a CSV dialect CsvSniffer.Detect infers the delimiter, quote character, and encoding (from a leading byte-order mark) from a sample of bytes, so a ;-separated pt-BR export or a TSV can be read without the caller knowing the dialect up front. It is deterministic (ties break by candidate order) and never throws on arbitrary input — an indecisive sample returns CsvDialect.Default (comma, ", UTF-8). using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader.Csv; CsvDialect dialect = CsvSniffer.DetectFile("export.csv"); using var csv = Excel.FromCsvFile("export.csv", new ExcelReaderOptions { Csv = CsvReaderOptions.Default.WithDialect(dialect) }); CsvSniffer.Detect takes a span of bytes or a seekable Stream, DetectFile takes a path, and DetectAsync/DetectFileAsync are the async siblings; only the first 64 KiB are examined. The Stream overloads require a seekable source — they read a bounded sample and restore the stream's position — so a non-seekable stream throws ArgumentException; buffer it first, or pass the bytes as a span instead. Pass CsvSnifferOptions to change the candidate delimiters/quotes (and their priority order) or the number of sample lines considered. CsvReaderOptions.SniffDialect does the sample-then-apply above for you, at the entry point that owns the source — the Excel.FromCsv* factories, and Excel.Open with ExcelFileFormat.Csv. The dialect of a parallel read is the one the CSV workbook was opened with: using var csv = Excel.FromCsvFile("export.csv", new ExcelReaderOptions { Csv = CsvReaderOptions.Default with { SniffDialect = true } }); An explicitly set Encoding survives sniffing unless the source carries a byte-order mark naming a different one — a sniffed encoding only ever comes from a BOM, so it never silently overrides a caller who knows their file is Windows-1252. Write CSV CsvWorkbookWriter emits RFC 4180 CSV: no styles or shared strings, so rows stream straight to the output. A CSV file is a single sheet, so AddSheet is called once (the name is ignored). using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Csv; using var stream = File.Create("out.csv"); using var workbook = CsvWorkbookWriter.Create(stream); using var writer = workbook.AddSheet("Sheet1"); using (CsvRowWriter row = writer.StartRow()) { row.Write("Name"); row.Write("Total"); row.Write("Created"); } using (CsvRowWriter row = writer.StartRow()) { row.Write("Q1"); row.Write(42); row.Write(DateTime.UtcNow); } Fields are quoted only when they contain the delimiter, quote character, \r, or \n; embedded quotes are doubled. bool writes as lowercase true/false and DateTime/DateOnly as round-trip ISO 8601 ("O"); TimeOnly as a time-of-day fraction — all matching what ExcelParser<T>.Parse(CsvSheet) expects, so a file written by CsvWorkbookWriter parses back without configuration. Skip(count) writes empty fields to keep column positions aligned (CSV has no sparse-cell concept). CsvWriterOptions mirrors CsvReaderOptions's delimiter, quote and encoding, so a file written with one set of settings reads back with the matching set: using var workbook = CsvWorkbookWriter.Create(stream, leaveOpen: false, new CsvWriterOptions { Delimiter = (byte)';', Encoding = Encoding.Latin1, // fields are formatted as UTF-8, then transcoded on the way out WriteByteOrderMark = true, // what makes Excel open a UTF-8 file as UTF-8 NewLine = CsvNewLine.LineFeed, // default is CRLF, as RFC 4180 specifies }); Fields containing \r or \n are quoted whichever NewLine is chosen, so the terminator never changes how the file reads back. To dump a collection of typed records instead of writing cells by hand, call WriteRecordsAsync on the sheet from CsvWorkbookWriter.Create(stream) — the same record-writing API as the Excel formats, restricted to a single sheet.

docs/guide/encryption.html.title: Encrypted workbooks | ExcelReader
docs/guide/encryption.html.summary: Encrypted workbooks Reading and writing password-protected packages. Encrypted workbooks Password-protected .xlsx/.xlsb/.xlsm files open through the same entry points — the password goes on the options, so every overload supports it: var options = new ExcelReaderOptions { Password = "hunter2" }; using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("protected.xlsx", options); foreach (Row row in workbook.FirstSheet) { /* ... */ } ExcelEncryptionException.Reason tells you what to do about a failure — only PasswordRequired and PasswordIncorrect are worth re-prompting for: try { using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open(path, options); } catch (ExcelEncryptionException ex) when (ex.Reason is ExcelEncryptionReason.PasswordIncorrect) { // Ask again. UnsupportedScheme and IntegrityFailure are terminal. } Supported: ECMA-376 agile encryption (Excel 2010+ — what Excel writes today when you set a password) and ECMA-376 standard encryption (Excel 2007 — AES-ECB with SHA-1). Not supported: RC4 CryptoAPI encryption, encrypted legacy .xls, and sheet/workbook protection passwords — a different mechanism entirely, stored as hashes in the plaintext XML. Password never appears in ExcelReaderOptions.ToString(). Note that a password supplied as a string cannot be wiped from memory — .NET strings are immutable and movable — so the library zeroes only the buffers it owns: the derivation buffer and the derived key. The dataIntegrity HMAC is not verified by default when reading from a stream. ExcelReaderOptions.VerifyEncryptedIntegrity defaults to false, because the HMAC covers the whole encrypted package: checking it means a full pass over the file before the first row, which makes time-to-first-row proportional to file size and defeats streaming. With it off, decryption still fails loudly on corrupt ciphertext (the plaintext stops being a valid ZIP), but targeted tampering by someone who can modify the file is not detected. Set it to true whenever the workbook comes from somewhere you do not control and you care that it was not altered: var options = new ExcelReaderOptions { Password = "hunter2", VerifyEncryptedIntegrity = true, // pay one full pass; reject tampered packages }; The in-memory path (Excel.Open(ReadOnlyMemory<byte>) and friends) has already decrypted everything by the time it returns, so it always verifies regardless of this setting. Standard encryption has no HMAC field, so the setting does not apply to it. Opening an encrypted workbook costs a fixed ~25 ms for key derivation, whatever the file size. After that, reading is ~3% slower than reading the same workbook unencrypted — see Encrypted workbooks in the benchmarks. Writing an encrypted workbook is a second step: build the package with any writer, then wrap it with Excel.EncryptPackage, which produces an agile-encrypted (ECMA-376 4.4) CFB container — AES-256-CBC, SHA-512, 100,000 spin iterations, with a dataIntegrity HMAC. using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Xlsx; using var plain = new MemoryStream(); var workbook = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(plain, leaveOpen: true); await using (workbook.ConfigureAwait(false)) { // write sheets and rows as usual } plain.Position = 0; using var destination = File.Create("secret.xlsx"); await Excel.EncryptPackageAsync(plain, destination, "hunter2").ConfigureAwait(false); The package stream must be seekable (it is read twice, so the container never has to be buffered in memory); the destination does not. Path-to-path overloads exist for both the sync and async forms. Encryption parameters are fixed at Excel's own defaults — there are no knobs — and only XLSX/XLSB packages can be encrypted, matching what the reader can decrypt.

docs/guide/errors.html.title: Errors across languages | ExcelReader
docs/guide/errors.html.summary: Errors across languages The .NET library throws exceptions. The C ABI turns each failure into an XL_* status code, and the Python, Rust and C++ bindings turn that code into their own error type. This page maps one onto the other, so a failure seen in one language can be recognized in another. Status codes Every xl_* function returns one of these. After a failure, xl_last_error_ptr returns the message for the calling thread. Code Constant Meaning 0 XL_OK Success. -1 XL_EOF No more rows or batches. Not an error: the bindings end iteration on it. -2 XL_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL The caller's buffer cannot hold the result. The bindings grow the buffer and retry, so it never reaches user code. -3 XL_INVALID_HANDLE The handle is null, already closed, or was never opened. -4 XL_INVALID_ARGUMENT An argument failed validation before any work started: a null pointer, a bad length, malformed options. -5 XL_ERROR Anything else. The message is the message of the .NET exception behind it. -6 XL_STATUS_PASSWORD_REQUIRED The workbook is encrypted and no password was supplied. -7 XL_STATUS_PASSWORD_INCORRECT The supplied password did not match the workbook's verifier. By failure Failure C# Status Python Rust C++ Encrypted, no password ExcelEncryptionException, Reason == PasswordRequired -6 PasswordRequiredError Error::PasswordRequired xl::Error, code == XL_STATUS_PASSWORD_REQUIRED Wrong password ExcelEncryptionException, Reason == PasswordIncorrect -7 PasswordIncorrectError Error::PasswordIncorrect xl::Error, code == XL_STATUS_PASSWORD_INCORRECT Unsupported encryption, or failed integrity check ExcelEncryptionException, Reason is UnsupportedScheme or IntegrityFailure -5 ExcelReaderError Error::Native xl::Error, code == XL_ERROR Corrupt or malformed file InvalidDataException -5 ExcelReaderError Error::Native xl::Error, code == XL_ERROR Feature the reader does not support NotSupportedException -5 ExcelReaderError Error::Native xl::Error, code == XL_ERROR File exceeds a configured resource limit ExcelLimitExceededException -5 ExcelReaderError Error::Native xl::Error, code == XL_ERROR Workbook already closed ObjectDisposedException -3 ExcelReaderError Error::Native xl::Error, code == XL_INVALID_HANDLE Invalid argument ArgumentException and its subclasses -4, or -5 when the check happens past the ABI boundary ExcelReaderError Error::Native xl::Error PasswordRequiredError and PasswordIncorrectError derive from ExcelReaderError, so except ExcelReaderError catches every native failure in Python. Rust's Error::code() returns the status for every variant. The C++ header throws nothing: every entry point returns std::expected<T, xl::Error>. Only the two password cases are worth retrying with different input. The rest fail the same way on every attempt. Each binding also checks some arguments itself, before calling the ABI, and reports those with its own native types: Python raises ValueError, TypeError or IndexError; Rust panics on an out-of-range index (see the crate README's "Bounds and panics"); C++ returns xl::Error with code == XL_INVALID_ARGUMENT.

docs/guide/migrating-to-v6.html.title: Migrating from v5 to v6 | ExcelReader
docs/guide/migrating-to-v6.html.summary: Migrating from v5 to v6 What changed in the reading API and how to port v5 code. See also reading.md for the full reading guide. What changed A v5 reader owned one "current sheet" that you moved with MoveToSheet; in v6 the reader became a workbook that hands out sheets, and each sheet is read on its own. Because a sheet no longer shares a cursor with its workbook, the sheets of one workbook can now be read in parallel. Types v5 v6 XlsxReader, XlsbReader, XlsReader XlsxWorkbook, XlsbWorkbook, XlsWorkbook XlsxReader.Enumerator (and the other two) XlsxWorkbook.Enumerator (and XlsbWorkbook.Enumerator, XlsWorkbook.Enumerator) IExcelRowReader IExcelWorkbook and IExcelSheet IExcelRowReader<TEnumerator> IExcelSheet<TEnumerator> ExcelSheet, reader.Sheets() XlsxSheet / XlsbSheet / XlsSheet / CsvSheet, workbook.Sheets CsvReader CsvReader (same name; now a workbook with one sheet) An explicit ExcelEnumerable<T, XlsReader, XlsReader.Enumerator> declaration becomes ExcelEnumerable<T, XlsSheet, XlsWorkbook.Enumerator> (likewise for XLSX and XLSB). A sheet is a small value (XlsxSheet and its siblings are readonly structs) that holds no resources: it is a workbook plus an index. IExcelSheet is the format-agnostic view of one, with Index, Name, Visibility and GetEnumerator(). Members v5 v6 reader.GetEnumerator(), foreach (Row row in reader) workbook.FirstSheet.GetEnumerator(), foreach (Row row in workbook.FirstSheet) reader.MoveToSheet(i) then read read workbook.Sheets[i] (workbook.SheetAt(i) on an IExcelWorkbook) reader.TryMoveToSheet(name) workbook.TryGetSheet(name, out var sheet) reader.SheetName, reader.SheetNameAt(i) sheet.Name, workbook.Sheets[i].Name reader.SheetVisibility, reader.SheetVisibilityAt(i) sheet.Visibility reader.SheetCount workbook.Sheets.Count (or workbook.SheetCount on IExcelWorkbook) parser.Parse(reader) parser.Parse(workbook.FirstSheet) Excel.InferSchema(reader) Excel.InferSchema(sheet) new ExcelDataReader(reader) new ExcelDataReader(sheet) reader.ToArrowRecordBatch() sheet.ToArrowRecordBatch() Excel.Open(...) returning IExcelRowReader Excel.Open(...) returning IExcelWorkbook; use FirstSheet, SheetAt(i) and TryGetSheet FirstSheet is the same sheet as Sheets[0] and SheetAt(0). Before and after Reading the first sheet: // v5 using IExcelRowReader reader = Excel.Open("book.xlsx"); foreach (Row row in reader) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } // v6 using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("book.xlsx"); foreach (Row row in workbook.FirstSheet) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } Walking every sheet: // v5 using IExcelRowReader reader = Excel.Open("book.xlsx"); for (int i = 0; i < reader.SheetCount; i++) { reader.MoveToSheet(i); Console.WriteLine(reader.SheetName); foreach (Row row in reader) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } } // v6 using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("book.xlsx"); for (int i = 0; i < workbook.SheetCount; i++) { IExcelSheet sheet = workbook.SheetAt(i); Console.WriteLine(sheet.Name); foreach (Row row in sheet) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } } When you open a format directly (Excel.FromXlsxFile and the like), workbook.Sheets is a typed list: foreach (XlsxSheet sheet in workbook.Sheets) walks every sheet without boxing. v5's ExcelSheet had a positional Deconstruct, so foreach (var (i, name) in reader.Sheets()) worked. The v6 sheets do not deconstruct; read the properties instead: foreach (XlsxSheet sheet in workbook.Sheets) { Console.WriteLine($"{sheet.Index}: {sheet.Name}"); } Parsing a named sheet: // v5 using IExcelRowReader reader = Excel.Open("changes.xlsx"); if (reader.TryMoveToSheet("Changes")) { foreach (ChangeRow item in ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ChangeRow>().Parse(reader)) { Console.WriteLine(item.File); } } // v6 using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("changes.xlsx"); if (workbook.TryGetSheet("Changes", out var sheet)) { foreach (ChangeRow item in ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ChangeRow>().Parse(sheet)) { Console.WriteLine(item.File); } } A CSV file: // v5 using CsvReader csv = Excel.FromCsvFile("book.csv"); foreach (Row row in csv) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } // v6 using CsvReader csv = Excel.FromCsvFile("book.csv"); foreach (Row row in csv.FirstSheet) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } Reading sheets in parallel Each sheet of a workbook can be read on its own thread: using XlsxWorkbook workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile(path); Parallel.For(0, workbook.Sheets.Count, i => { foreach (Row row in workbook.Sheets[i]) { // consume } }); The contract: A workbook is safe to share between threads once it is open: reading its metadata, getting sheets and creating enumerators all work concurrently. An enumerator belongs to one thread at a time. Using one enumerator from two threads at once is undefined behavior and is not checked. You may have several enumerators open at once, including several over the same sheet. The exception is a CSV over a non-seekable stream, which serves one. Do not use, reposition or dispose a stream or buffer you passed in until the workbook and every enumerator obtained from it are disposed. Behavior changes Getting a workbook's sheets (Sheets, FirstSheet, SheetAt, TryGetSheet) or opening an enumerator after Dispose throws ObjectDisposedException (since 5.2.0). SheetCount and IsDate1904 still answer. Disposing a workbook does not close its file or stream while an enumerator from it is still undisposed; the resources are released when the last enumerator is disposed (since 5.2.0). A failed XLSX shared-string load fails every later enumeration the same way (since 5.2.0). A cancelled XLSX shared-string load is retried by the next enumeration, and the bytes it had read still count toward MaxTotalDecompressedBytes (since 5.2.0). A CSV over a seekable stream is read from the position the stream had when the CsvReader was created, by any number of enumerators at once. The stream's position afterwards is unspecified: file streams and memory streams with an exposed buffer are left untouched, any other seekable stream may be moved (since 5.2.0). A CSV over a non-seekable stream still allows one enumeration (since 5.2.0). Native bindings The C ABI changes with the library: XL_ABI_VERSION is 6. A workbook handle no longer has a current sheet. Every read takes a zero-based sheet index, and rows are read through a cursor opened per sheet, so one handle serves several threads. v5 v6 xl_open_file(path, len, format, &wb) xl_open_file(path, len, format, NULL, &wb) xl_open_file_ex, xl_open_memory_ex xl_open_file, xl_open_memory with the options pointer xl_move_to_sheet(wb, i) pass i to the read function xl_sheet_name(wb, ...) xl_sheet_name_at(wb, i, ...) none xl_sheet_visibility_at(wb, i, &v), xl_sheet_index(wb, name, len, &i) xl_next_row(wb, ...) xl_rows_open(wb, i, &rows), xl_rows_next(rows, ...), xl_rows_close(rows) xl_next_row_view(wb, &row) xl_rows_next_view(rows, &row) xl_read_all_blob(wb, ...), xl_read_all_decoded(wb, &out) xl_rows_read_all_blob(rows, ...), xl_rows_read_all_decoded(rows, &out) xl_rows (the decoded result struct) xl_rows_decoded; xl_rows is now the cursor handle xl_parse_typed(wb, specs, n, header, &t) xl_parse_typed(wb, i, specs, n, header, 1, &t) xl_parse_typed_ex(wb, specs, n, header, dop, &t) xl_parse_typed(wb, i, specs, n, header, dop, &t) xl_parse_arrow, xl_parse_arrow_ex xl_parse_arrow(wb, i, specs, n, header, dop, &array, &schema) xl_parse_arrow_stream(wb, ...), xl_typed_reader_open(wb, ...) the same, with i after wb xl_infer_schema(wb, header, sample, &s) xl_infer_schema(wb, i, header, sample, 0, &s) xl_infer_schema_ex(wb, header, sample, flags, &s) xl_infer_schema(wb, i, header, sample, flags, &s) Behavior changes: xl_parse_typed and xl_parse_arrow used to read sequentially; pass 1 as degree_of_parallelism to keep that. 0 uses every processor on a CSV. Opening a second typed reader or Arrow stream on a workbook used to fail, and reading the workbook another way used to invalidate an open one. Both now work: each read is independent. A cursor, typed reader or Arrow stream keeps working after xl_close on its workbook. Rust The crate follows the library: reads move from Workbook to Sheet. v5 v6 workbook.move_to_sheet(i)? then a read workbook.sheet(i)? and read from it workbook.sheet_name()? workbook.sheet(i)?.name()? or workbook.sheet_name_at(i)? workbook.rows() workbook.sheet(0)?.rows()? workbook.read_all_blob()?, read_all_decoded()? the same methods on a Sheet workbook.typed_chunks::<T>(h, n)?, workbook.infer_schema(h, n)? the same methods on a Sheet parse_sheet::<T>(&mut workbook, h)? parse_sheet::<T>(workbook.sheet(0)?, h)? parse_arrow::<T>(&mut workbook, h)?, parse_arrow_stream the same, taking a Sheet Workbook no longer needs to be mut, and it is Send + Sync. A cursor reads its sheet once from the top; call rows() again for another pass. Sheet::read_all_blob() and read_all_decoded() read the whole sheet from its first row; they no longer continue a cursor. A crate built for ABI 5 refuses a v6 library with an ABI-version error at the first Workbook::open. Python The package follows the library: reads move from Workbook to Sheet. v5 v6 workbook.move_to_sheet(i) then a read read from workbook.sheets[i] workbook.sheet_name workbook.sheets[i].name for index, name in workbook.sheets(): for sheet in workbook.sheets: workbook.rows(), read_all(), read_all_columnar() the same methods on workbook.sheets[i] workbook.parse_typed(...), to_arrow(...), to_polars(...), infer_schema(...) and the other read methods the same methods on workbook.sheets[i], same arguments workbook.sheets["Name"] finds a sheet by name and raises KeyError when there is none. A package built for ABI 5 refuses a v6 library when it loads it. Each rows() call starts at the sheet's first row, and read_all() / read_all_columnar() read the whole sheet; none of them continues an earlier read. A rows() generator that has started keeps working after workbook.close(), where v5 raised. C++ The wrapper follows the library: reads move from xl::Workbook to xl::Sheet. v5 v6 workbook.move_to_sheet(i) then a read read from workbook.sheet(i) workbook.sheet_name() workbook.sheet(i).name() or workbook.sheet_name_at(i) workbook.rows() workbook.sheet(0).rows(), which returns std::expected<RowCursor, Error> workbook.read_all_decoded(), workbook.infer_schema(h, n) the same methods on a Sheet xl::parse_sheet<T>(workbook, h), xl::typed_reader<T>(workbook, h, n) the same, taking a Sheet xl::parse_arrow<T>(workbook, h), xl::arrow_stream<T>(workbook, h, n) the same, taking a Sheet rows() then next_row() then read_all_decoded() auto cursor = sheet.rows(); cursor->next_row(); cursor->read_all_decoded(); xl::RowCursor now owns a native cursor and is move-only. Sheet::read_all_decoded() reads the whole sheet from its first row; to read what a cursor has left, call RowCursor::read_all_decoded(). Code built against the v5 header does not link or load against a v6 library, because the v5 exports it names are gone.

docs/guide/migrating-to-v7.html.title: Migrating from v6 to v7 | ExcelReader
docs/guide/migrating-to-v7.html.summary: Migrating from v6 to v7 What changed in parallel reading and in the rest of the public API, and how to port v6 code. See also reading.md for the full guide. What changed Parallel reading now takes a sheet, and it works on XLSX and XLSB as well as CSV. CsvParallel is gone: its eighteen path, memory and stream methods became six SheetParallel methods that take any IExcelSheet. You open the workbook yourself, pass its sheet, and the library parallelises as far as the format allows. The contract types lost their Csv prefix because they now serve every format. Types v6 v7 CsvParallel SheetParallel CsvParallelOptions SheetParallelOptions (no Reader property) ICsvRecord<TSelf> IRowRecord<TSelf> ICsvAccumulator<TSelf, TModel> IRowAccumulator<TSelf, TModel> CsvAggregation<TState> RowAggregation<TState> CsvRowAction<TState> RowAction<TState> The old names are removed, with no [Obsolete] forwarders. Members, contracts and results are unchanged. Before and after A CSV file: // v6 await foreach (Sale s in CsvParallel.ParseAsync(path, parser, new CsvParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8, Reader = options })) { Total += s.Revenue; } // v7 using CsvReader csv = Excel.FromCsvFile(path, new ExcelReaderOptions { Csv = options }); await foreach (Sale s in SheetParallel.ParseAsync(csv.FirstSheet, parser, new SheetParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8 })) { Total += s.Revenue; } CSV bytes in memory: // v6 await foreach (Sale s in CsvParallel.ParseAsync(data, parser, new CsvParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8, Reader = options })) { Total += s.Revenue; } // v7 using CsvReader csv = Excel.FromCsv(data, new ExcelReaderOptions { Csv = options }); await foreach (Sale s in SheetParallel.ParseAsync(csv.FirstSheet, parser, new SheetParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8 })) { Total += s.Revenue; } A stream: // v6 await foreach (Sale s in CsvParallel.ParseAsync(stream, parser, new CsvParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8, Reader = options })) { Total += s.Revenue; } // v7 using CsvReader csv = Excel.FromCsv(stream, leaveOpen: true, new ExcelReaderOptions { Csv = options }); await foreach (Sale s in SheetParallel.ParseAsync(csv.FirstSheet, parser, new SheetParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8 })) { Total += s.Revenue; } The other five methods port the same way: open a workbook, pass csv.FirstSheet (or any sheet) in place of the path, bytes or stream, and drop Reader from the options. XLSX and XLSB need no other change: using XlsxWorkbook workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("big.xlsx"); await foreach (Sale s in SheetParallel.ParseAsync(workbook.FirstSheet, parser, new SheetParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8 })) { Total += s.Revenue; } Behavior changes The caller owns the workbook and keeps it open until the task completes or the enumeration ends. v6 opened and closed its own source. The CSV dialect is given when the workbook is opened (ExcelReaderOptions.Csv), not in the parallel options. A CSV in a MemoryStream is no longer partitioned: the stream overload of Excel.FromCsv reads it sequentially. Pass the bytes as ReadOnlyMemory<byte> to keep partitioning. HeaderRow rules are the same as v6. ParseAsync takes the header from ExcelParserOptions.HeaderRow and rejects a non-zero SheetParallelOptions.HeaderRow; the parser-based ForEachAsync and AggregateAsync use SheetParallelOptions.HeaderRow. XLSX and XLSB sheets are now read on several threads when DegreeOfParallelism allows it. XLS, a table view (ExcelTable.AsSheet()), a sheet under 256 KB uncompressed and a CSV that cannot be partitioned still read sequentially with the same results. PrefetchDecompression does not apply to a parallel XLSX or XLSB read; the pipeline already overlaps inflate and parse. Other breaking changes These changes replace positional parameters and loose arguments with types that can grow without another break. v6 v7 ExcelParserConfig ExcelParserOptions; the ExcelParser factories' parameter is options IExcelCellConverter<T>.TryConvert(in Cell, bool isDate1904, IFormatProvider provider, out T) TryConvert(in Cell, in ExcelRowContext context, out T) ExcelCellReader<T>, ExcelRowParser<T>, ExcelCellReaders.*: (…, bool isDate1904, IFormatProvider provider, …) (…, in ExcelRowContext context, …) Excel.InferSchema(sheet, headerRow, sampleSize, parseText) returning ExcelColumnSchema[] Excel.InferSchema(sheet, new SchemaInferenceOptions { HeaderRow = …, SampleSize = …, ParseText = … }) returning IReadOnlyList<ExcelColumnSchema> new ExcelDataReader(sheet, headerRow) new SheetDataReader(sheet, new SheetDataReaderOptions { HeaderRow = … }) sheet.ToArrowRecordBatch(schema, headerRow) sheet.ToArrowRecordBatch(new ArrowReadOptions { Schema = schema, HeaderRow = … }) WriteRecordBatch(batch, sheetName, writeHeader) and the async form WriteRecordBatch(batch, new ArrowWriteOptions { SheetName = …, WriteHeader = … }) XlsWorkbookWriter.Create(stream, leaveOpen, date1904) XlsWorkbookWriter.Create(stream, leaveOpen, new XlsWriterOptions { Date1904 = … }) Excel.FromCsv*(…, CsvReaderOptions options) Excel.FromCsv*(…, new ExcelReaderOptions { Csv = options }) CsvReaderOptions.MaxCellBytes, CsvReaderOptions.InternStrings ExcelReaderOptions.MaxCellBytes, ExcelReaderOptions.InternStrings CellType.Formula Removed. A formula cell reports its cached result's type: Number, Date, ExcelString, Boolean or Error ExcelDataReader (its name collided with Sylvan.Data.Excel and the ExcelDataReader package) SheetDataReader Cell.TryGetDateTime(out DateTime), which silently assumed the 1900 date system Cell.TryGetDateTime(workbook.IsDate1904, out DateTime) A converter reads the date system and culture from the context: // v6 public bool TryConvert(in Cell cell, bool isDate1904, IFormatProvider provider, out decimal value) => decimal.TryParse(cell.GetString(), NumberStyles.Currency, provider, out value); // v7 public bool TryConvert(in Cell cell, in ExcelRowContext context, out decimal value) => decimal.TryParse(cell.GetString(), NumberStyles.Currency, context.FormatProvider, out value); To unit-test a converter, build the context with an initializer: new ExcelRowContext { IsDate1904 = false, FormatProvider = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture }. Two behavior changes come with them: Excel.Open with ExcelFileFormat.Csv now applies ExcelReaderOptions.MaxCellBytes and InternStrings. v6 ignored both and used the CSV defaults. Formula cells are typed by their cached result in every format. v6 reported an XLSX text result and an XLS numeric result as Formula, so an XLS formula with a date style lost its Date type, and XLSB never used Formula. The CLI convert command no longer shifts dates by four years when the source workbook uses the 1904 date system. XlsxWriterOptions gains Date1904, which v6 lacked. It defaults to false, so existing output is unchanged. Stricter reading and writing v7 refuses several inputs that v6 accepted and then got wrong. Damaged packages. Each ZIP entry of an XLSX or XLSB package is checked against its CRC-32. A mismatch throws InvalidDataException when the entry's last byte is read, so rows before the damage may already have been returned. v6 checked only the entry's size. Set ExcelReaderOptions.VerifyZipChecksums to false to read a package whose producer wrote wrong checksums; the bindings have the same switch as verify_zip_checksums. The check costs 2% to 4% of a read, and under 1% with PrefetchDecompression, where it runs on the background thread. Line breaks in XLSX text. A cell with a line break now reads with , as XLSB and XLS already did. Excel stores the break as a CR LF pair in the XML, which v6 returned as . A carriage return stored as data (_x000D_ or ) is still returned. Code that split XLSX text on should split on . Sheet names. AddSheet throws ArgumentException for a name that begins or ends with an apostrophe, or contains a control character (tab and line feed included), U+FFFE or U+FFFF. Excel refuses a workbook with such a name. Column settings. SetColumnWidth and SetColumnStyle throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException for a column past the format's last one (16,384 columns; 256 for XLS) and for a width above 255, Excel's maximum. v6 wrote a file Excel refused for the first, and an XLS width of 256 came out as a hidden column. Number formats. AddStyle throws ExcelLimitExceededException for the 201st distinct number format of a workbook, and ArgumentException for a format longer than 255 characters. Excel does not open a workbook past either. Rows in XLSB. A sheet stops at 1,048,576 rows. v6 accepted one more, which Excel does not read. Values with no numeric form. Write<T> with a type that does not convert to a number, such as char, throws ArgumentException in every writer. XLSB and XLS threw InvalidCastException. Text in XLSX. A carriage return, U+FFFE and U+FFFF in cell text are now written escaped. v6 wrote them raw: Excel read the carriage return as a line feed and refused a file with either of the other two. ExcelLimitExceededException.Message no longer says "bytes" for limits counted in rows, columns or entries. LimitName, Limit and Actual are unchanged. Native bindings The C ABI is unchanged: no signature moved, and XL_ABI_VERSION stays 6. Behavior changed. degree_of_parallelism of 0 on xl_parse_typed and the Arrow exports now parallelises XLSX and XLSB as well as CSV, using every processor. Pass 1 for the old sequential behavior. The Rust, Python and C++ bindings take the same value (degree_of_parallelism, parallelism) and need no code change; a parallelism=0 call on an XLSX or XLSB sheet is now faster, and holds every partition's columns until they merge, so its peak memory is higher. XL_CELL_FORMULA (5) is no longer produced; formula cells come back with their result's cell type. The constant stays defined in the header and in the bindings. xl_write_options.date1904 now applies to XLSX as well as XLSB and XLS; v6 ignored it for XLSX. xl_csv_aggregate keeps its signature. Inside, it opens a CsvReader with the dialect from the native struct and calls SheetParallel. Python: one way to open a workbook open_bytes() is removed. open_workbook() takes the bytes instead, and also accepts a bytearray, a memoryview or an io.BytesIO. It also takes a Source or a readable stream, the inputs that 7.0's release candidates opened with open_source() and open_stream(), which are gone as well. Arguments and keywords are unchanged. v6 v7 open_bytes(data, "xlsx", password=p) open_workbook(data, "xlsx", password=p) open_bytes(buffer.getvalue()) open_workbook(buffer) Python: one way to write a workbook write_workbook_to_bytes(), write_arrow_to_bytes(), write_pandas_to_bytes() and write_polars_to_bytes() are removed. write_workbook(), write_arrow(), write_pandas() and write_polars() take the destination first, a path or a binary object with write(), such as io.BytesIO. A destination without a path needs format. The frame writers now take format and options as keywords instead of passing **kwargs through. v6 v7 payload = write_workbook_to_bytes(table, types, format="xlsx") buffer = io.BytesIO() write_workbook(buffer, table, types, format="xlsx") payload = buffer.getvalue() write_pandas_to_bytes(df, format="xlsx") write_pandas(buffer, df, format="xlsx") The streaming writer and the encryption helper follow the same pattern. open_writer_to_memory() and SheetWriter.bytes() are removed: open_writer() takes a binary object with write() and hands it the finished workbook when the writer closes. encrypt_package_bytes() is removed: encrypt_package() takes the package as a path, bytes or io.BytesIO, and the destination as a path or an object with write(). v6 v7 with open_writer_to_memory("xlsx") as w: ... payload = w.bytes() buffer = io.BytesIO() with open_writer(buffer, "xlsx") as w: ... payload = buffer.getvalue() secret = encrypt_package_bytes(payload, password) encrypt_package(payload, out, password) with out = io.BytesIO() Python: one shape per read A sheet reads as rows (rows()), a typed table (parse_typed(), or iter_parse_typed() in batches), Arrow (to_arrow(), or to_arrow_stream() in batches) or a DataFrame (to_pandas(), to_polars()). write_workbook() takes a TypedTable or any Arrow-compatible table, including pandas and polars DataFrames. SheetWriter writes whole rows only. v6 v7 workbook.sheet_count len(workbook.sheets) workbook.sheet_names [s.name for s in workbook.sheets] workbook.sheet_name_at(i) workbook.sheets[i].name sheet.read_all() list(sheet.rows()), or parse_typed() for speed sheet.read_all_columnar(), ColumnarSheet, decode_cell() sheet.parse_typed(sheet.infer_schema()) sheet.to_arrow() returning a StructArray sheet.to_arrow() returns a pyarrow.RecordBatch sheet.to_record_batch(...) sheet.to_arrow(...) sheet.to_record_batch_reader(...) pyarrow.RecordBatchReader.from_stream(sheet.to_arrow_stream(...)) sheet.iter_pandas(...), sheet.iter_polars(...) iterate the reader above and convert each batch write_arrow(dest, batch), write_pandas(dest, df), write_polars(dest, df) write_workbook(dest, batch_or_df) writer.start_row(), write_str(v) … write_timestamp(v), end_row() writer.write_row([...]) writer.write_null(ColumnType.X) (None, ColumnType.X) as a value in write_row OpenOptions(csv_max_cell_bytes=n), OpenOptions(csv_intern_strings=b) OpenOptions(max_cell_bytes=n), OpenOptions(intern_strings=b), which now apply to CSV too from excelreader import ArrowStream from excelreader.arrow_stream import ArrowStream Python: value types are not tuples Cell, ColumnSpec, OpenOptions, WriteOptions and TypedTable are frozen dataclasses instead of named tuples, so a field added in a later version breaks no caller. They cannot be unpacked or indexed, and fields are passed by name; ColumnSpec keeps type as its one positional argument. open_writer() takes options as a keyword. Python 3.10 or later is required. v6 v7 column, type_, value = cell cell.column, cell.type, cell.value ColumnSpec(ColumnType.I64, "qty") ColumnSpec(ColumnType.I64, name="qty") open_writer(dest, "xlsx", opts) open_writer(dest, "xlsx", options=opts) C++: one overload set per operation Workbook::open takes a path, a byte span, a Source or an InputStream. write_columns, write_sheet and WriterHandle::open take a path or a std::vector<std::uint8_t>&. Options are passed as const Options& = {}, and the format moved into OpenOptions::format and WriteOptions::format (XL_FORMAT_AUTO infers it from a path's extension). v6 v7 Workbook::open(path, format, &opts) Workbook::open(path, {.format = format, ...}) Workbook::open_memory(span, ...), open_source(...), open_stream(...) The raw C interface (Xl*, xl_*, XL_*) is private, and integer codes became the enums Format, ColumnType and ErrorKind.
