docs/guide/parsing.html.title: Typed parsing | ExcelReader
docs/guide/parsing.html.summary: Typed parsing Binding worksheet or CSV rows to your own types: attributes, the compile-time generator, the fluent API, converters, and the zero-copy ref struct path. Parse typed rows ExcelParser.FromAttributes<T>() maps worksheet columns to the public settable properties of T. Columns match on the property name, or on [ExcelColumn("header")] aliases — repeat the attribute to accept several headers. The first row is the header by default. using ExcelReader.Core.Parser; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; public sealed class ChangeRow { [ExcelColumn("file")] public string File { get; set; } = ""; [ExcelColumn("lines_added")] public int LinesAdded { get; set; } } using var workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("changes.xlsx"); var parser = ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ChangeRow>(); foreach (var item in parser.Parse(workbook.FirstSheet)) { Console.WriteLine($"{item.File}: +{item.LinesAdded}"); } Built-in property types: string, bool, DateTime, DateOnly, TimeOnly, TimeSpan, DateTimeOffset, Guid, char, every integral and floating type plus decimal, and enums (matched by member name or numeric value). Each also works as a Nullable<T>. Empty cells leave the property at its default; an unparseable cell is skipped (keeps the default) unless the column is required. T needs no parameterless-constructor constraint, so models with required members are supported, through both FromAttributes and the source generator. required alone does not make a column mandatory; that is what [ExcelRequired] does. Parse also accepts the IExcelSheet of the IExcelWorkbook from Excel.Open, so you can parse without knowing the concrete format: using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("changes.xlsx"); // or .xlsb / .xls foreach (var item in ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ChangeRow>().Parse(workbook.FirstSheet)) { /* ... */ } Generate typed maps at compile time (Native AOT / trimming) ExcelParser.FromAttributes<T> and ExcelRecordLayout.FromAttributes<T> reflect over T (GetProperties, MakeGenericMethod), which trimming can break and Native AOT cannot run at all. The raw Excel.From* readers already use no reflection; mark a model [ExcelSerializable] to get the same guarantee for the typed layer — a source generator emits a compile-time map from the model's own [ExcelColumn]/[ExcelRequired]/[ExcelConverter]/[ExcelIgnore] attributes, and ExcelParser.Generated<T>/ExcelRecordLayout.Generated<T> read and write through that map instead of reflection: using ExcelReader.Core.Parser; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Xlsx; [ExcelSerializable] // the model must be declared partial public partial class ChangeRow { [ExcelColumn("file")] public string File { get; set; } = ""; [ExcelColumn("lines_added")] public int LinesAdded { get; set; } } using var workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("changes.xlsx"); foreach (var item in ExcelParser.Generated<ChangeRow>().Parse(workbook.FirstSheet)) { Console.WriteLine($"{item.File}: +{item.LinesAdded}"); } var changes = new[] { new ChangeRow { File = "README.md", LinesAdded = 12 } }; await using var stream = File.Create("changes.xlsx"); await using var writer = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(stream); // or XlsbWorkbookWriter / XlsWorkbookWriter / CsvWorkbookWriter await using (var sheet = writer.AddSheet("Changes")) { await sheet.WriteRecordsAsync(changes, ExcelRecordLayout.Generated<ChangeRow>()); } Notes: [ExcelSerializable] requires the model — and every type it's nested inside, if any — to be partial; the generator emits into an additional part of the same declaration. A compile error (EXR001/EXR002) names exactly what to fix. Supported property types match ExcelParser.FromAttributes<T>'s: string, bool, DateTime, DateOnly, TimeOnly, TimeSpan, DateTimeOffset, Guid, char, every integral and floating type plus decimal, enums, and Nullable<T> of each — plus ReadOnlySpan<byte>, which binds zero-copy through ExcelCellReaders.Utf8. The model may be a ref struct: mark it ref partial struct and the generator emits IExcelRowMap<T> on it like any other shape, so ExcelParser.Generated<T> and ExcelParser.Build<T> read it AOT-clean, as do the map-driven SheetParallel.ForEachAsync/SheetParallel.AggregateAsync overloads. The generator requires a build via dotnet build/the .NET SDK. Visual Studio's or MSBuild.exe's .NET Framework host can't load it, so a project built only through those tools won't see generated code — build via the SDK, or fall back to ExcelParser.FromAttributes<T>/ExcelRecordLayout.FromAttributes<T> for that build path. ExcelParser.Generated<T> builds one map per model and reuses it for every reader, including CSV — unlike ExcelParser.FromAttributes<T>, which swaps in a text-based date reader specifically for CSV. A [ExcelSerializable] model reads DateTime/DateOnly/TimeOnly via ExcelCellReaders.DateTimeAuto/DateOnlyAuto/TimeOnlyAuto: an Excel serial number first, falling back to date/time text when the cell isn't numeric — so a CSV column round-trips through the library's own writer either way. The one edge case this can't distinguish: a CSV cell that's only digits (e.g. an Excel serial number typed as plain text) is always read as a serial number, never as date text. The attribute-based reflection path keeps working unchanged; [ExcelSerializable] is an additive, opt-in alternative for the same model shape, not a replacement. Map columns at runtime (fluent API) [ExcelColumn]/[ExcelRequired] fix the mapping at compile time. When the mapping itself is a runtime decision — loaded from a config file, chosen by a user in a UI, or different per input file — build it with ExcelRowMapBuilder<T> through ExcelParser.Build<T> instead: using ExcelReader.Core.Parser; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; public sealed class ChangeRow { public string File { get; set; } = ""; public int LinesAdded { get; set; } } var parser = ExcelParser.Build<ChangeRow>(builder => builder .Factory(() => new ChangeRow()) .Property(["file"], ExcelCellReaders.String, (ref ChangeRow r, string v) => r.File = v) .Property(["lines_added"], ExcelCellReaders.Parsable, (ref ChangeRow r, int v) => r.LinesAdded = v)); using var workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("changes.xlsx"); foreach (var item in parser.Parse(workbook.FirstSheet)) { Console.WriteLine($"{item.File}: +{item.LinesAdded}"); } The map is built once, when Build is called, from a fresh builder instance — never from a static per-type cache, so two parsers configured differently for the same T give different, correct results in the same process. Bind a fixed column index instead of a header name with PropertyAt — for files with no header row at all: var parser = ExcelParser.Build<ChangeRow>(builder => builder .Factory(() => new ChangeRow()) .PropertyAt(0, ExcelCellReaders.String, (ref ChangeRow r, string v) => r.File = v) .PropertyAt(1, ExcelCellReaders.Parsable, (ref ChangeRow r, int v) => r.LinesAdded = v)); A builder that uses PropertyAt skips the header-row step entirely — the first row is already data. Mixing PropertyAt with Property/PropertyNullable/Converted on the same builder throws, since one map can't both wait for a header row and skip it. ExcelParser.BuildWithAttributeFallback<T> merges the builder's bindings with [ExcelColumn]/[ExcelRequired]-driven ones reflected from T: a builder binding replaces every attribute-driven property that shares one of its header names; a property whose header names none of the builder's bindings mention keeps its attribute-driven behavior. Useful for overriding just the one column that's a runtime decision without redeclaring the whole model — reuse one of the property's existing [ExcelColumn] names in the builder: var parser = ExcelParser.BuildWithAttributeFallback<ChangeRow>(builder => builder .Property(["file"], ExcelCellReaders.String, (ref ChangeRow r, string v) => r.File = v.ToUpperInvariant())); The match is by header name, not by property identity: configuring a different header name for File would not override its attribute — both bindings would survive and File would be assigned twice on the same row. Build is AOT-clean — configure is caller-written code wiring hand-picked readers and setters, no reflection. BuildWithAttributeFallback also reflects over T for the fallback half, so it carries the same [RequiresUnreferencedCode]/[RequiresDynamicCode] annotations as FromAttributes. Parser configuration Pass an ExcelParserOptions to control header handling and culture: using System.Globalization; using ExcelReader.Core.Parser; var options = new ExcelParserOptions { HeaderRow = 1, // 1-based row holding the headers ColumnNameComparer = StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase, HeaderNormalization = HeaderNormalization.Trim | HeaderNormalization.CollapseSpaces, Culture = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("pt-BR"), // parse "1.234,56" as 1234.56m }; var parser = ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ChangeRow>(options); Culture applies when parsing text-backed numeric/Guid cells (XLSX inline and shared strings); binary numeric cells (XLS/XLSB) carry a raw value and ignore it. HeaderNormalization flags (Trim, CollapseSpaces, RemoveDiacritics) are applied to both the sheet headers and the property names before matching. Required columns Mark a property [ExcelRequired] to assert its column exists and carries a value: public sealed class Order { [ExcelRequired] public int Id { get; set; } [ExcelRequired(AllowEmpty = true)] // column must exist; blank cells allowed public string? Note { get; set; } } A missing required header throws when the header row is read, listing every missing column. By default each data row must have a non-empty cell; the first blank throws, naming the column and row number. AllowEmpty = true relaxes this to column presence only. The check covers presence, not parseability — a present-but-malformed value does not throw here. Custom converters For types the built-in parsers do not handle — money strings, custom formats, domain value objects — implement IExcelCellConverter<T> and attach it with [ExcelConverter]. T must be the property's exact type. One instance is created and reused across all rows, so converters must be stateless. using System.Globalization; using ExcelReader.Core.Parser; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; public sealed class BrlMoneyConverter : IExcelCellConverter<decimal> { public bool TryConvert(in Cell cell, in ExcelRowContext context, out decimal value) { string text = cell.GetString().Replace("R$", "", StringComparison.Ordinal).Trim(); return decimal.TryParse(text, NumberStyles.Currency, CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("pt-BR"), out value); } } public sealed class Invoice { [ExcelConverter(typeof(BrlMoneyConverter))] public decimal Total { get; set; } } Return false to signal a parse failure (the property keeps its default). Empty cells are skipped before the converter runs. context carries the workbook's date system (IsDate1904) and the parser culture (FormatProvider); to unit-test a converter, pass new ExcelRowContext { IsDate1904 = false, FormatProvider = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture }. Parse into a ref struct (zero-copy) ExcelParser.FromAttributes<T> takes a ref struct model just as it takes a class or a struct — same attribute-driven column matching ([ExcelColumn], [ExcelRequired], [ExcelConverter]), but a ReadOnlySpan<byte> property binds directly to the cell's raw bytes instead of allocating a string: using System.Text; using ExcelReader.Core.Parser; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; public readonly ref struct ChangeRowRef { public ReadOnlySpan<byte> File { get; init; } // zero-copy — aliases the reader's row buffer public int LinesAdded { get; init; } } using var workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("changes.xlsx"); foreach (ChangeRowRef item in ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ChangeRowRef>().Parse(workbook.FirstSheet)) { Console.WriteLine($"{Encoding.UTF8.GetString(item.File)}: +{item.LinesAdded}"); } The result of Parse supports await foreach (add .WithCancellation(ct) to pass a token), so a ref struct model can be parsed asynchronously — the rows are streamed via MoveNextAsync while the model stays a zero-copy ref struct: await using var workbook = await Excel.FromXlsxFileAsync("changes.xlsx"); await foreach (ChangeRowRef item in ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ChangeRowRef>().Parse(workbook.FirstSheet)) { Console.WriteLine($"{Encoding.UTF8.GetString(item.File)}: +{item.LinesAdded}"); } A few differences from a class or struct model: Span fields alias the reader's row buffer — valid only until the next row. Copy them out (e.g. Encoding.UTF8.GetString(span)) if you need to keep the value past the loop body. Under await foreach, the same rule means the model can't be held across an await in the loop body. The non-generic IEnumerator.Current throws. IEnumerable<T> and IAsyncEnumerable<T> both accept a ref struct element type on net9.0+, so the sequence flows through them normally; only the legacy non-generic IEnumerator.Current cannot, because it would have to box. LINQ over a ref struct model is still out, since its operators do not carry the allows ref struct anti-constraint. Not AOT/trim-safe on this path, since it reflects over T's properties and compiles setters at runtime. For an AOT-clean zero-copy model, mark the ref partial struct [ExcelSerializable] and read it with ExcelParser.Generated<T> — see Generate typed maps at compile time. A regular struct/class model uses the same entry point — only a genuine ref struct model gets the extra zero-copy span-property binding.

docs/guide/reading.html.title: Reading rows | ExcelReader
docs/guide/reading.html.summary: Reading rows Opening a workbook, enumerating rows, and the async and prefetch paths. See also parsing.md for binding rows to types, and csv.md for delimited text. Read rows using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; using var workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("report.xlsx"); foreach (var row in workbook.FirstSheet) { string name = row[0].GetString(); if (row[1].TryParse(null, out int quantity)) { Console.WriteLine($"{name}: {quantity}"); } if (row[2].Type == CellType.Date && row[2].TryGetDateTime(workbook.IsDate1904, out var date)) { Console.WriteLine(date); } } An opened workbook (XlsxWorkbook, XlsbWorkbook, XlsWorkbook, CsvReader) hands out its sheets: FirstSheet is the first one, Sheets[i] any of them. A sheet holds no resources of its own; iterating it starts a new, independent read. Dispose the workbook, not the sheets. Parallel reading (opt-in) SheetParallel reads one sheet on several threads. It takes any sheet, so it works the same on XLSX, XLSB and CSV: using XlsxWorkbook workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("big.xlsx"); await foreach (var row in SheetParallel.ParseAsync(workbook.FirstSheet, ExcelParser.FromAttributes<SalesRow>(), new SheetParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8 })) { Total += row.Revenue; } You own the workbook: keep it open until the task completes or the enumeration ends. For CSV, give the dialect when you open it (Excel.FromCsvFile(path, options)), not in the options. DegreeOfParallelism of 0 (the default) uses every processor; 1 reads sequentially. There are three families, each over a sheet: Family Result Order ParseAsync<T> an IAsyncEnumerable<T> the sheet's own order, identical to parser.Parse(sheet) ForEachAsync calls your callback on the worker threads none AggregateAsync folds one accumulator per partition into a result the same result as a single-threaded run Parsing and type conversion run across threads; whatever your loop body does per row does not, so if that dominates, raising the degree will not help. Both of the next two examples read a ref struct model, so text columns stay as ReadOnlySpan<byte> and the per-row model allocation disappears; a class model still costs one instance per row. A fold over an XLSX sheet, with one accumulator per partition merged in sheet order: public ref struct SaleRow { [ExcelColumn("Region")] public ReadOnlySpan<byte> Region { get; set; } [ExcelColumn("Units")] public int Units { get; set; } } public sealed class UnitTotal : IRowAccumulator<UnitTotal, SaleRow> { public long Units; public void Add(SaleRow model) => Units += model.Units; public void Merge(UnitTotal following) => Units += following.Units; } using XlsxWorkbook workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("big.xlsx"); UnitTotal total = await SheetParallel.AggregateAsync<UnitTotal, SaleRow>( workbook.FirstSheet, ExcelParser.FromAttributes<SaleRow>(), new SheetParallelOptions { HeaderRow = 1 }); The same call takes a RowAggregation<TState> when you would rather pass delegates than write a type, and an IRowRecord<TRecord> type in place of the parser. A per-row callback: using XlsxWorkbook workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("big.xlsx"); long total = 0; await SheetParallel.ForEachAsync( workbook.FirstSheet, ExcelParser.FromAttributes<SaleRow>(), row => Interlocked.Add(ref total, row.Units), new SheetParallelOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 8, HeaderRow = 1 }); Unlike ParseAsync, the callback runs on the worker threads, so records arrive in no particular order and the callback must be safe to call from several threads at once. Spans are valid only for the duration of the call. HeaderRow follows the same rule as before: ParseAsync takes the header from the parser's ExcelParserOptions.HeaderRow and rejects a non-zero SheetParallelOptions.HeaderRow, while the parser-based ForEachAsync and AggregateAsync use SheetParallelOptions.HeaderRow. When it reads sequentially These cases read on one thread with the same results and no error: DegreeOfParallelism of 1. A sheet under 256 KB uncompressed. XLS. A table view (ExcelTable.AsSheet()). A CSV that cannot be partitioned: a stream that is not a file, or a non-UTF-8 encoding. Only in-memory data (ReadOnlyMemory<byte>, byte[]) and a FileStream-backed source partition; a CSV over a MemoryStream does not, so pass its bytes as ReadOnlyMemory<byte>. PrefetchDecompression does not apply on this path: XLSX and XLSB go through a pipeline that already overlaps inflate and parse. Delivery guarantees ParseAsync and AggregateAsync are exact on every format. ParseAsync yields the same items in the same order as the sequential parse; AggregateAsync equals its own single-threaded run. XLSB delivers every row exactly once, in ForEachAsync too. XLSX delivers exactly once for a well-formed sheet. The pipeline cuts the inflated sheet at what looks like a row start; on a sheet where those bytes sit inside cell content (a CDATA run, a comment) or the file is truncated, a worker detects it, and the read recovers by reading the rest sequentially. ParseAsync and AggregateAsync stay exact. In ForEachAsync, workers may already have called the callback for chunks that are then dropped, so on such a sheet rows can be delivered twice, or be rows the sequential reader would not produce. CSV delivers exactly once when it follows RFC 4180 quoting (every quote opens or closes a quoted field, or is doubled inside one) and no quoted field is longer than 64 KB. A partition's start is read off the quotes around it, and a partition whose quotes could open as well as close a field waits for its confirmed start instead of being guessed. CSV outside those rules (a stray quote inside an unquoted field, text after a closing quote, a quoted field past 64 KB) is at least once in ForEachAsync: the callback may be invoked more than once for the same record. A partition whose start offset was guessed wrongly is read again from the confirmed offset, and the discarded pass may already have delivered a whole partition's worth of records, 1 MiB to 64 MiB of them, not just a few near the seam. Those records may also be misparsed, carrying values that appear nowhere in the file, and an exception the callback threw during a discarded pass is discarded with it. For exactly once on any source, use AggregateAsync, where the discarded partition's accumulator is thrown away, and apply side effects once it returns. A callback that writes to a database or sends messages must be idempotent on a CSV that may break those rules, and on XLSX if the sheet may be malformed, and must also tolerate records that do not exist: deduplicating on a key does not filter those out. ExcelParseException.Row on ParseAsync counts the rows emitted so far. On ForEachAsync and AggregateAsync it is the row a sequential read reports, whether or not the read was partitioned. See the parallel sheet benchmarks and the parallel CSV benchmarks for what this buys. On a real-data XLSX the sheet stage drops from 24 ms (prefetched, sequential) to about 17 ms, and on XLSB from 17 ms to about 13 ms; the floor is inflate, which runs on one thread. CSV has no such floor: its AggregateAsync at dop 4 is ~2.0x faster than the typed path while allocating ~630x less, with zero garbage collections. Properties need setters. A get-only property is skipped during binding and silently receives nothing. Apache Arrow conversion (opt-in) dotnet add package ExcelReader.Arrow using ExcelReader.Arrow; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; using var workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("report.xlsx"); Apache.Arrow.RecordBatch batch = workbook.FirstSheet.ToArrowRecordBatch(); The schema defaults to Excel.InferSchema's guess; pass one in new ArrowReadOptions { Schema = ... } to skip inference, and set HeaderRow there (default 1, 0 for none). The whole sheet is materialized into one RecordBatch — there is no chunked/streaming variant yet. Inference costs about the same time and ~1.8x the allocation of an explicit schema on the same file. See Arrow conversion in the benchmarks. WriteRecordBatch/WriteRecordBatchAsync are the write-side mirror — one call from a RecordBatch to a sheet, for XLSX, XLSB, XLS, and CSV: using ExcelReader.Arrow; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Xlsx; using XlsxWorkbookWriter workbook = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(File.Create("report.xlsx")); workbook.WriteRecordBatch(batch); // adds the sheet, writes the header + every row, ends the workbook Supports string, large string, string view, every integer width (signed and unsigned), half float, float, double, decimal128, decimal256, boolean, date32, date64, time32, time64, timestamp and null columns; any other type (binary, nested, dictionary) throws NotSupportedException. Pass new ArrowWriteOptions { WriteHeader = false } to skip the header row, or set SheetName (XLSX/XLSB/XLS only — CSV has no sheet name) to rename it from the "Sheet1" default. Open by auto-detecting the format Excel.Open picks the workbook type from the file signature (XLSX/XLSB are ZIP packages, XLS is an OLE2 document) and returns an IExcelWorkbook. FirstSheet gives the first sheet, and a sheet iterates its rows directly, so no pattern-match is needed for basic row iteration. using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("report.xlsx"); // or report.xlsb / report.xls foreach (var row in workbook.FirstSheet) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } SheetCount, SheetAt(index) and TryGetSheet(name) are on IExcelWorkbook itself, so you can walk every sheet without knowing the format. Each IExcelSheet carries its own Index, Name and Visibility: using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("report.xlsx"); for (int i = 0; i < workbook.SheetCount; i++) { IExcelSheet sheet = workbook.SheetAt(i); Console.WriteLine(sheet.Name); foreach (var row in sheet) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } } TryGetSheet matches a name ignoring case and opens nothing: if (workbook.TryGetSheet("Totals", out var totals)) { foreach (var row in totals) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } } When you open a format directly (Excel.FromXlsxFile and the like) the workbook's Sheets is a typed, indexable list (Sheets.Count, Sheets[i], foreach) of XlsxSheet, XlsbSheet or XlsSheet values, so walking it boxes nothing. Reaching a sheet only looks up a name and an index; the file is not read until you iterate the sheet. Visibility reports whether a sheet is shown in the workbook's tab bar, read from the format's own encoding of it (XLSX's state attribute, XLSB's BrtBundleSh.hsState, XLS's BoundSheet8.hsState). It is reported, never enforced — a hidden sheet enumerates its rows like any other, so converters and exporters filter on it themselves: using ExcelReader.Core; // ExcelSheetVisibility, shared by the readers and writers for (int i = 0; i < workbook.SheetCount; i++) { IExcelSheet sheet = workbook.SheetAt(i); if (sheet.Visibility != ExcelSheetVisibility.Visible) { continue; // skip hidden and veryHidden sheets } Console.WriteLine(sheet.Name); } ExcelSheetVisibility.VeryHidden is the state Excel's own unhide dialog does not offer; both it and Hidden come back here. A sheet whose format says nothing about its state — or says something no producer agrees on — reads as Visible. CSV is exposed as a single, unnamed sheet (SheetCount == 1, Name == "", always Visible). Pattern-match to the concrete type only for workbook-specific internals beyond this surface. OpenAsync is the async counterpart. Both require a seekable stream (or a file path) so the signature can be read without consuming the input. Detection covers the signed formats only. To open a source whose format you already know — including CSV, which has no signature to detect — pass an ExcelFileFormat and let ExcelReaderOptions.Csv carry the dialect; see CSV. using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("report.csv", ExcelFileFormat.Csv); Read an Excel table A workbook's tables (ranges formatted with Format as Table) are listed on Tables, ordered by sheet and creation, and found by name with TryGetTable, ignoring case. XLSX/XLSM and XLSB report them; XLS and CSV always report none. AsSheet() reads only the table: its header row first, then its data rows without the totals row, each cut to the table's columns, so it plugs into anything that takes a sheet. using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("sales.xlsx"); if (workbook.TryGetTable("Sales", out ExcelTable? sales)) { foreach (ProductRow row in ExcelParser.FromAttributes<ProductRow>().Parse(sales.AsSheet())) { Console.WriteLine($"{row.Product}: {row.Qty}"); } } FirstRow, FirstColumn, LastRow and LastColumn are zero-based and include the header and totals rows; Ref is the same range in A1 notation. Column indexes inside AsSheet() rows stay those of the sheet: a table starting at column C reports its first cell at index 2. Excel.InferSchema keeps those indexes in ExcelColumnSchema.Index but lists only the table's columns. SheetDataReader ordinals are relative to the table: ordinal 0 is its first column. A table whose header row is turned off (HeaderRowCount == 0) still enumerates, but Parse throws InvalidOperationException for every map, and SheetDataReader and InferSchema throw it when HeaderRow is greater than 0. Read it with new SheetDataReader(table.AsSheet(), new SheetDataReaderOptions { HeaderRow = 0 }), Excel.InferSchema(table.AsSheet(), new SchemaInferenceOptions { HeaderRow = 0 }), or by column index on the rows. StyleName is the table style's name, such as TableStyleMedium2, or null when the table has none. Reading sheets in parallel This is one thread per sheet. To read a single sheet on several threads, see Parallel reading. Each sheet of a workbook can be read on its own thread: using XlsxWorkbook workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile(path); Parallel.For(0, workbook.Sheets.Count, i => { foreach (Row row in workbook.Sheets[i]) { // consume } }); The contract: A workbook is safe to share between threads once it is open: reading its metadata, getting sheets and creating enumerators all work concurrently. An enumerator belongs to one thread at a time. Using one enumerator from two threads at once is undefined behavior and is not checked. You may have several enumerators open at once, including several over the same sheet. Do not touch a stream you passed in while the workbook is open. Disposing the workbook closes it to new sheets and enumerators; its file or stream is released when the last enumerator already obtained from it is disposed. Read asynchronously Every sheet supports await foreach. For XLSX files, the async enumerator buffers one row at a time and uses the same row parser as the synchronous enumerator, so sync and async reads stay behaviorally aligned while awaits happen only when more bytes are needed. using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; await using var workbook = await Excel.FromXlsxFileAsync("report.xlsx", ct: cancellationToken); await foreach (var row in workbook.FirstSheet) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } await foreach binds to the sheet's GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken ct = default) by pattern. The call itself does no I/O: opening the sheet part (and, for XLSX, loading shared strings) happens asynchronously on the first MoveNextAsync. Because Row and Cell are ref struct types, the current row cannot be held across an await inside the loop body: read its cells (or copy the values out) before awaiting anything else. await foreach does not accept .WithCancellation(ct): Row being a ref struct rules out IAsyncEnumerable<Row>, so the loop binds to the pattern rather than the interface. To pass a token, or to await while a row is in scope, drive the enumerator manually: await using var workbook = await Excel.FromXlsxFileAsync("report.xlsx", ct: cancellationToken); await using var rows = workbook.FirstSheet.GetAsyncEnumerator(cancellationToken); while (await rows.MoveNextAsync()) { var row = rows.Current; Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } Errors from opening the sheet, such as cancellation or a corrupt part, surface from that first MoveNextAsync, not from GetAsyncEnumerator. Prefetch decompression (XLSX/XLSB) XLSX and XLSB are ZIP-backed, and inflating a sheet's compressed bytes competes for wall-clock time with parsing it. ExcelReaderOptions.PrefetchDecompression overlaps the two: a background thread inflates ahead while the calling thread parses. It is opt-in, defaults to false, and only affects XLSX/XLSB — XLS and CSV have nothing to decompress, so the option is silently ignored for them. var options = new ExcelReaderOptions { PrefetchDecompression = true }; using var workbook = Excel.FromXlsxFile("report.xlsx", options); foreach (var row in workbook.FirstSheet) { Console.WriteLine(row[0].GetString()); } Measured across both read benchmarks (see Real data reads and String-heavy reads), on 65K-row workbooks: Workload Default PrefetchDecompression = true Gain XLSX, real data 37.2 ms 23.7 ms 36% XLSM, real data 38.0 ms 23.1 ms 39% XLSB, real data 24.7 ms 16.6 ms 33% XLSX, string-heavy 30.0 ms 20.0 ms 33% XLSB, string-heavy 33.6 ms 19.5 ms 42% The gain tracks how much of a read is decompression rather than parsing, so it is smallest on XLSB real data and string-heavy XLSX (about a third) and largest on string-heavy XLSB (42%). Allocations rise from the producer task and the pooled decompression buffers — on the real-data corpus, roughly 7 KB to 23 KB for XLSX and 7 KB to 15 KB for XLSB — and neither path triggers a garbage collection. Do not enable it for concurrent server workloads: a caller already reading many files in parallel is CPU-saturated, and an extra background thread per read only doubles thread demand for no gain. It's meant for single-file batch processing. Writing has the same option, under a different name: see Prefetch compression. Bridge to ADO.NET (IDataReader) SheetDataReader adapts one IExcelSheet to System.Data.IDataReader, so it drops straight into SqlBulkCopy, DataTable.Load, Dapper, or any other ADO.NET consumer: using System.Data; using ExcelReader.Core.Reader; using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open("report.xlsx"); using IDataReader data = new SheetDataReader(workbook.FirstSheet); // header on row 1 by default var table = new DataTable(); table.Load(data); The header row (1-based, default 1) fixes the column shape; pass new SheetDataReaderOptions { HeaderRow = 0 } for a header-less sheet, whose columns come back named Column0, Column1, ... sized from the first data row. There is no schema-inference pass — GetFieldType/GetValue/the typed getters read the current row's own cell type, so a consumer building its schema from the first row (like DataTable.Load) locks in that row's types for the whole load. NextResult() always returns false; build one SheetDataReader per sheet instead of chaining result sets. The bridge costs ~1.3–1.4x over iterating rows directly, and GetBytes stays within ~10% of the direct read. See ADO.NET bridge in the benchmarks.

docs/guide/untrusted-input.html.title: Reading untrusted files | ExcelReader
docs/guide/untrusted-input.html.summary: Reading untrusted files What one hostile workbook can cost you, which options bound it, and how to reject a file cleanly. Read this before you accept spreadsheets from uploads, APIs or mail. A spreadsheet is a container whose sizes, counts and offsets are written by whoever made the file. The readers check every one of those values before it drives an allocation, and the options below turn what is left — a file that is well-formed but simply enormous — into an ExcelLimitExceededException instead of an out-of-memory crash. The defaults suit a desktop tool or a batch job reading files you trust. A server should set its own. The limits All of them live on ExcelReaderOptions: Option Default Bounds Formats MaxTotalDecompressedBytes 512 MiB What one read of a sheet inflates or loads from its container, counting the workbook's metadata, styles, shared strings and decrypted package XLSX, XLSB, XLS, encrypted MaxSharedStringBytes 128 MiB The shared-string table, which is held in memory for the whole read XLSX, XLSB, XLS MaxCellBytes 32 MiB Each buffer that grows to hold one cell value, or one CSV record all MaxZipEntries 65,536 Entries in the ZIP directory XLSX, XLSB MaxPasswordSpinCount 100,000 Key-derivation iterations an agile-encrypted file may ask for encrypted XLSX, XLSB Two limits are fixed by Excel's grid rather than configured: a cell past column XFD (16,384) throws with LimitName == "Columns", and no single buffer may exceed .NET's array size (LimitName == "ArrayMaxLength"). How they count: MaxTotalDecompressedBytes is per read of a sheet. The workbook's one-time loads (its metadata, styles and shared strings) count toward every read, and each read adds the sheet it inflates. Reading a sheet again starts from the one-time loads, so a workbook kept open and read repeatedly never runs out. XLS has nothing to inflate, but it is not streamed: the whole Workbook stream is read into memory, up to MaxTotalDecompressedBytes. CSV has no total limit. It streams, so the size of what you hand it is the bound; only MaxCellBytes applies. Zero or a negative value turns a byte or entry limit off. MaxPasswordSpinCount has no off switch. In the Python, Rust and C++ bindings and the C ABI, 0 means the default instead, and a limit cannot be turned off. Reads running at once each have their own budget. Ten uploads read together, or several sheets of one workbook read on different threads, can inflate ten times the budget between them. A profile for uploads Size each limit for the largest file you legitimately expect, measured rather than guessed. For a service taking spreadsheets of a few MB, something like: var uploadOptions = new ExcelReaderOptions { MaxTotalDecompressedBytes = 64L * 1024 * 1024, // everything one workbook may inflate MaxSharedStringBytes = 16L * 1024 * 1024, MaxCellBytes = 1024 * 1024, MaxZipEntries = 1_000, }; Cap the upload itself as well, before it reaches the reader: the options bound what the file expands to, not how many bytes you accept. Excel.Open needs a seekable stream, so buffer a request body to a file or to memory first. Leave PrefetchDecompression off: it adds a thread per read, which a busy server cannot spare. For encrypted uploads, set VerifyEncryptedIntegrity so a tampered package is rejected; see Encrypted workbooks. No option bounds wall-clock time. The work a read does grows with the bytes it inflates, which the limits bound; for a deadline, use the async entry points and enumerators, which take a CancellationToken. Rejecting a file A limit can trip when the workbook opens, when you start reading a sheet (XLSX loads its shared strings then), or halfway down it. Wrap the whole read, not just the open, and do not commit rows until the read has finished: try { using IExcelWorkbook workbook = Excel.Open(upload, options: uploadOptions); foreach (Row row in workbook.FirstSheet) { // stage the row; commit only once the loop has finished } } catch (ExcelLimitExceededException ex) { Console.WriteLine($"Rejected: {ex.LimitName} reached {ex.Actual}, limit {ex.Limit}"); } catch (Exception ex) when (IsRejectedFile(ex)) { Console.WriteLine($"Rejected: {ex.Message}"); } static bool IsRejectedFile(Exception ex) { return ex is InvalidDataException or EndOfStreamException or NotSupportedException or ExcelEncryptionException or ExcelParseException || ex.GetType() == typeof(ArgumentException) || ex.GetType() == typeof(InvalidOperationException); } LimitName is the option's name (or Columns, ArrayMaxLength); Limit and Actual are in that limit's unit — bytes, entries or iterations. That exception list is exactly what the fuzz suite accepts as a correct rejection of arbitrary bytes. Anything else escaping a read of a file — an IndexOutOfRangeException, an OutOfMemoryException, a hang — is a bug; please report it privately as described in SECURITY.md. See Errors across languages for how these map onto the bindings. Damaged packages An XLSX or XLSB package is a ZIP archive, and each of its entries carries a CRC-32 of its data. The reader checks it as the entry is read and throws InvalidDataException on a mismatch, so a file cut short or altered in transit does not come back as plausible but wrong cells. A sheet is checked when its last byte is read, which means the rows before the damage may already have been returned: treat the exception as invalidating everything read from that file. The checksum guards against accidents, not tampering, since whoever alters the data can recompute it. ExcelReaderOptions.VerifyZipChecksums turns the check off. What the reader does not do It evaluates nothing. A formula cell reports the result Excel cached when it saved the file, so the value is whatever the file claims; recompute anything you rely on. Macros are never run and external links never followed. It resolves no XML entities beyond the predefined ones. Sheet XML goes through the library's own scanner, which decodes &-style and numeric references and copies anything else through as text, so there is no entity expansion and no external fetch. The one XmlReader, for the encryption descriptor, prohibits DTDs. Writing untrusted text to CSV The writers store text as text: in XLSX, XLSB and XLS a string that starts with = is still a string. CSV has no cell types, and Excel opening a .csv treats a field starting with =, +, - or @ as a formula. CsvWorkbookWriter writes your text unchanged, so if a person may open the file in a spreadsheet program, neutralize those fields yourself: static string Neutralize(string text) { return text.Length > 0 && "=+-@\t\r".Contains(text[0]) ? "'" + text : text; } row.Write(Neutralize(comment)); The leading ' changes the data, so do this only for files meant for people, not for files another program parses back.

docs/guide/versioning.html.title: Versioning and compatibility | ExcelReader
docs/guide/versioning.html.summary: Versioning and compatibility What a new version can change, and how to write code that keeps compiling and running across minor versions. The .NET packages follow Semantic Versioning: a major version (7.0, 8.0) may break your code, while a minor (7.1) or a patch (7.0.1) does not. What a minor version may add New types, new members on existing types, and new overloads. New properties on the options objects, such as ExcelReaderOptions. A new option always defaults to the previous behavior. New members on the interfaces that only this library implements (below). New values in the enums (below). Bug fixes. A file that used to read wrong, or a written file that Excel refused or altered, can come out differently after a fix. Other changes in what an existing call returns or throws wait for a major version and are listed in its migration guide. A minor version does not remove or rename anything, change an existing signature, or add a parameter to an existing method. Interfaces you implement These are the extension points. A minor version never adds a member to them that you would have to implement: IExcelCellConverter<T> and IExcelCellWriter<T> IExcelRowMap<T> and IExcelRecordMap<T> IRowRecord<TSelf> and IRowAccumulator<TSelf, TModel> New information reaches them through the types they already receive. For example, a converter gets it as a new member of ExcelRowContext, not as a new parameter. Interfaces only the library implements The reading and writing interfaces describe what every format's workbook, sheet and row writer can do. Program against them, but do not implement them: IExcelWorkbook, IExcelSheet and IExcelSheet<TEnumerator> IExcelRowEnumerator IWorkbookWriter<TSheet>, ISheetWriter<TRow>, ITableSheetWriter<TRow> and IRowWriter A minor version can add members to them. Each new member comes with a default implementation, so an existing implementation still compiles and loads, but it throws NotSupportedException or falls back to a slower path for the new member. A feature that only some formats support appears first on the concrete types (XlsxSheetWriter, XlsbWorkbook), or as a separate interface the way ITableSheetWriter<TRow> sits beside ISheetWriter<TRow>. Enums that grow CellType and ExcelColumnType can gain values in a minor version, as can their native counterparts XL_CELL_* and XL_T_*. An existing value never changes its number or meaning. A switch over them should have a default branch: string text = cell.Type switch { CellType.Empty => "", CellType.Number when cell.TryGetDouble(out double number) => number.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture), _ => cell.GetString(), }; The native library and the bindings The C ABI is versioned on its own by XL_ABI_VERSION, which xl_abi_version() reports. It changes only when a signature or a struct layout does: 7.0 kept version 6. Every options struct starts with struct_size, so a field added in a later version does not break a caller compiled against an earlier header. The Rust, Python and C++ bindings check the ABI version when they load the library. xl_write_options grew from 32 to 40 bytes after 7.0 (degree_of_parallelism and batch_rows, appended); the 7.0 size is still accepted and writes serially, so the ABI version stayed 6. 7.x also added xl_rows_foreach and xl_aggregate. They are new exports only, so the ABI version stayed 6; a binding built against them fails with a missing-symbol error when it loads an older ABI-6 library that lacks them. How it is enforced Every pull request packs ExcelReader.NET and ExcelReader.Arrow and compares them with the last release through .NET package validation. A removed or changed member fails the build.

docs/guide/writing.html.title: Writing workbooks | ExcelReader
docs/guide/writing.html.summary: Writing workbooks Writers for XLSX (Open XML), XLSB (BIFF12) and XLS (BIFF8), cell styles, typed records, and prefetch compression. See csv.md for CSV output. Write XLSX workbooks using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Xlsx; await using var stream = File.Create("out.xlsx"); await using var workbook = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(stream); await using (var sheet = workbook.AddSheet("Summary")) { await using (var row = await sheet.StartRowAsync()) { row.Write("Name"); row.Write("Total"); row.Write("Created"); } await using (var row = await sheet.StartRowAsync()) { row.Write("Q1"); row.Write(42); row.Write(DateTime.UtcNow); } } await workbook.EndAsync(); By default, the XLSX writer emits inline strings to keep memory usage flat while rows stream out. If your workbook repeats many strings and smaller files matter more than the extra lookup table, opt in to shared strings: await using var workbook = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(stream, options: new XlsxWriterOptions { UseSharedStrings = true }); Hidden sheets Every IWorkbookWriter<TSheet> takes an optional ExcelSheetVisibility alongside the sheet name, written to whatever the format uses for it — XLSX's state attribute, XLSB's BrtBundleSh.hsState, XLS's BoundSheet8.hsState — so it reads back through IExcelSheet.Visibility: using ExcelReader.Core; // ExcelSheetVisibility, shared by the readers and writers await using (var data = workbook.AddSheet("Data")) { /* rows */ } // visible await using (var lookups = workbook.AddSheet("Lookups", ExcelSheetVisibility.Hidden)) { /* rows */ } await using (var audit = workbook.AddSheet("Audit", ExcelSheetVisibility.VeryHidden)) { /* rows */ } // not in Excel's unhide dialog A workbook whose sheets are all hidden is rejected when it is ended (InvalidOperationException): the formats allow it, but Excel reports such a file as damaged, so it is caught at write time rather than shipped to a user. CSV accepts the argument and ignores it — delimited text has no tab bar to hide from. Cell styles on write Every IWorkbookWriter<TSheet> supports column- and row-level styling: a number format (currency, date, percentage), bold, and italic. Register a CellStyle once with AddStyle and apply its returned index to a column (before the first row) or to a whole row (when starting it): using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Xlsx; await using var workbook = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(stream); int currency = workbook.AddStyle(new CellStyle { NumberFormat = "R$ #,##0.00" }); int header = workbook.AddStyle(new CellStyle { Bold = true }); await using var sheet = workbook.AddSheet("Summary"); sheet.SetColumnStyle(columnIndex: 1, currency); // before the first row sheet.SetColumnWidth(columnIndex: 0, width: 20); await using (var row = await sheet.StartRowAsync(header)) { row.Write("Product"); row.Write("Total"); } await using (var row = await sheet.StartRowAsync()) { row.Write("Widget"); row.Write(1234.5); } await workbook.EndAsync(); AddStyle deduplicates by value: registering the same CellStyle twice returns the same index, and index 0 is always the general/default style. SetColumnStyle/SetColumnWidth must be called before the sheet's first StartRow/StartRowAsync (calling them later throws InvalidOperationException) — the column layout (XLSX <cols>, XLSB BrtColInfo, XLS COLINFO) has to be written ahead of the row data. A row's style (from StartRowAsync(int, CancellationToken)) takes precedence over its column's style for any cell in that row. CSV has no cell concept of style: every style member is a documented no-op there. Cell-level styling (one specific cell rather than a whole column or row) is out of scope. Bold/italic render only in XLSX today; XLSB and XLS apply the number format but keep the default font, since their font records are opaque binary blobs this library isn't confident hand-editing without a verified field map. Read and write XLSB workbooks (BIFF12) Use Excel.FromXlsbFile, Excel.FromXlsb, Excel.FromXlsbFileAsync, or Excel.FromXlsbAsync to open XLSB directly. For writing, use XlsbWorkbookWriter, XlsbSheetWriter, and XlsbRowWriter. using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Xlsb; await using var stream = File.Create("out.xlsb"); await using var workbook = XlsbWorkbookWriter.Create(stream); await using (XlsbSheetWriter sheet = workbook.AddSheet("Summary")) { await using (XlsbRowWriter row = await sheet.StartRowAsync()) { row.Write("Name"); row.Write("Total"); row.Write("Created"); } } await workbook.EndAsync(); The XLSB writer also defaults to inline string cells. Set XlsbWriterOptions.UseSharedStrings to deduplicate repeated text into sharedStrings.bin. Write XLS workbooks (BIFF8) XlsWorkbookWriter emits a binary BIFF8 .xls file. The sheet and row APIs are synchronous; only the final EndAsync (which assembles and flushes the OLE container) is async. BIFF8 is capped at 65,536 rows × 256 columns per sheet. using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Xls; await using var stream = File.Create("out.xls"); await using var workbook = XlsWorkbookWriter.Create(stream); using (var sheet = workbook.AddSheet("Summary")) { using (var row = sheet.StartRow()) { row.Write("Name"); row.Write("Total"); row.Write("Created"); } using (var row = sheet.StartRow()) { row.Write("Q1"); row.Write(42); row.Write(DateTime.UtcNow); } } await workbook.EndAsync(); Write typed records The low-level writers above give you cell-by-cell control. When you just want to dump a collection of objects to a sheet, sheet.WriteRecordsAsync(records, layout) writes a header row followed by one row per record, with the columns coming from an ExcelRecordLayout<T>. ExcelRecordLayout.FromAttributes<T>() maps each public readable property to a column by reflection. It is an extension on ISheetWriter<TRow>, so the same call works on a sheet from any of the writers above — XLSX, XLSB, XLS, and CSV. using ExcelReader.Core.Writer; using ExcelReader.Core.Writer.Xlsx; public sealed class Sale { public string? Region { get; set; } public int Units { get; set; } public decimal Revenue { get; set; } public DateOnly Date { get; set; } } var sales = new[] { new Sale { Region = "North", Units = 42, Revenue = 1234.50m, Date = new DateOnly(2026, 1, 2) }, new Sale { Region = "South", Units = 17, Revenue = 512.00m, Date = new DateOnly(2026, 1, 3) }, }; await using var stream = File.Create("sales.xlsx"); await using var workbook = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(stream); // or XlsbWorkbookWriter / XlsWorkbookWriter / CsvWorkbookWriter await using (var sheet = workbook.AddSheet("Sales")) { await sheet.WriteRecordsAsync(sales, ExcelRecordLayout.FromAttributes<Sale>()); } Disposing the sheet ends it; add the next sheet after that (a duplicate name throws, ignoring case), so one workbook can hold sheets of different record types. The sheet stays open after WriteRecordsAsync, so you can append more rows before disposing it. CsvWorkbookWriter is the exception: a CSV file is a single sheet, so a second AddSheet throws (the sheet name is ignored). An IAsyncEnumerable<T> overload streams records that are produced asynchronously. The written file round-trips straight back through ExcelParser<T> because the headers are the property names. Column behavior mirrors the parser attributes: [ExcelColumn("Header")] — use a custom header instead of the property name (the first alias wins). [ExcelIgnore] — exclude a property from both writing and parsing (for computed/transient members). [ExcelConverter(typeof(MyConverter))] — if the converter also implements IExcelCellWriter<T>, it controls how the value is written, so a custom type round-trips through the same converter it reads with. DateTime and DateOnly are written as Excel date serials; TimeOnly as a time-of-day fraction. Numeric properties (including Half) become number cells; any other type is written as text formatted with the invariant culture — DateTimeOffset as ISO 8601 ("O"), enums by name — so the file parses back the same whatever the writing machine's culture. Int128/UInt128 stay text because a number cell is a double and would drop their low digits. (CsvWorkbookWriter follows the CSV rules instead — see Write CSV — writing DateTime/DateOnly as ISO text and TimeOnly as a time-of-day fraction, all still round-tripping through ExcelParser<T>.) For a model marked [ExcelSerializable], pass ExcelRecordLayout.Generated<T>() instead — same behavior, but driven by the source-generated map instead of reflection, so it stays Native AOT/trim-safe. See Generate typed maps at compile time. Write an Excel table The XLSX and XLSB sheet writers implement ITableSheetWriter<TRow>. BeginTable writes the header row and opens a table there; every row written until EndTable (or the end of the sheet) belongs to it. The file opens in Excel already formatted as a table, with filter buttons and the chosen built-in style, and reads back through IExcelWorkbook.Tables. using XlsxWorkbookWriter workbook = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(File.Create("report.xlsx")); XlsxSheetWriter sheet = workbook.AddSheet("Report"); sheet.BeginTable("Sales", ["Region", "Units", "Revenue"]); foreach (Sale s in sales) { using XlsxRowWriter row = sheet.StartRow(); row.Write(s.Region); row.Write(s.Units); row.Write(s.Revenue); } sheet.EndTable(); For records, WriteTableAsync does all three steps with the same layouts as WriteRecordsAsync: await sheet.WriteTableAsync(sales, "Sales", ExcelRecordLayout.FromAttributes<Sale>()); ExcelTableOptions sets FirstColumn, StyleName (a built-in TableStyleLight1–21, TableStyleMedium1–28 or TableStyleDark1–11, or null for none; default TableStyleMedium2) and the banding flags ShowRowStripes, ShowColumnStripes, ShowFirstColumn, ShowLastColumn. With FirstColumn > 0, rows you write yourself must Skip(FirstColumn) to reach the table; WriteTableAsync does it for you. One table can be open per sheet at a time; write as many as you like one after another. Table names must be valid Excel names, must not read as cell references (A1, R1C1), and must be unique in the workbook, ignoring case. A table with no data rows gets one empty row, as Excel requires. Totals rows, custom table styles, and tables in XLS or CSV are not supported. Prefetch compression (XLSX/XLSB writing) The write-side mirror of Prefetch decompression. XLSX and XLSB are ZIP-backed, so every row a writer serializes has to be deflated before it reaches the stream, and by default that happens on the calling thread. Set PrefetchWrite on the writer options to move the deflate onto a background thread, so the caller keeps building the next batch of rows while the previous one compresses: await using var wb = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(stream, leaveOpen: true, options: new XlsxWriterOptions { PrefetchWrite = true }); XlsxSheetWriter sheet = wb.AddSheet("S1"); foreach (var record in records) { using XlsxRowWriter row = sheet.StartRow(); row.Write(record.Name); row.Write(record.Value); } await sheet.EndAsync(); XlsbWriterOptions has the same property. XLS and CSV are uncompressed, so they have nothing to overlap and do not offer it. Writing a 50,000-row workbook (WriteBenchmark): Workload Default PrefetchWrite = true Gain XLSX 8.191 ms 5.351 ms 35% XLSB 5.462 ms 3.282 ms 40% Allocations are unchanged (4.02 MB either way) — the background writer hands over buffers the row writer already owns rather than copying them. The same caveat as the read side applies: do not enable it for concurrent server workloads. A caller already writing many files in parallel is CPU-saturated, and an extra background thread per writer only doubles thread demand for no gain. It's meant for single-file batch work. Write records in parallel (XLSX/XLSB) PrefetchWrite moves compression off the calling thread, but the rows are still built on one thread, and building them is most of a write. WriteRecordsParallelAsync and WriteTableParallelAsync use several cores for both: the records are cut into batches, each batch is formatted and compressed on a pool thread, and the batches reach the file in order. They are extensions on XlsxSheetWriter and XlsbSheetWriter, and take an IEnumerable<T> or an IAsyncEnumerable<T>. The cell-by-cell API stays single-threaded, and XLS and CSV have no parallel form. await using var wb = XlsxWorkbookWriter.Create(stream, leaveOpen: true); XlsxSheetWriter sheet = wb.AddSheet("S1"); // Header row from the layout, then one row per record. await sheet.WriteRecordsParallelAsync(records, ExcelRecordLayout.FromAttributes<Metric>()); // Or format each row yourself; this delegate runs on several threads at once. await sheet.WriteRecordsParallelAsync(records, static (XlsxRowWriter row, Metric record) => { row.Write(record.Name); row.Write(record.Value); }, new ParallelWriteOptions { DegreeOfParallelism = 4 }); await sheet.EndAsync(); The rules: Your delegate runs on several threads at once, though never twice at once on the same row writer. Whatever it captures must be thread-safe. The library's own layouts are. Order is kept. Rows come out in the order the source yields them, and the source itself is enumerated by one flow at a time, never concurrently. Rows may be written before and after the call, not during it. Row numbering carries on, and the call can be made more than once on a sheet. A failure or a cancellation ends the sheet and the workbook. A serial WriteRecordsAsync cancelled between rows leaves the sheet usable; a parallel call does not. The original exception is rethrown once every batch in flight has stopped. With UseSharedStrings, string indexes depend on thread timing, so two runs give files that differ byte for byte. Their content is the same. More than 1,048,576 rows throws ExcelLimitExceededException. ParallelWriteOptions has two knobs. DegreeOfParallelism is the most batches in flight at once (0, the default, means one per core). BatchRows is the rows per batch, 8,192 by default. Memory grows with their product: at the defaults each batch in flight holds about 3 MB (its formatted rows, the compressor's window and the compressed result), whatever the size of the sheet. Writing 1,000,000 rows of four columns (text, integer, date, number) to a MemoryStream at Fastest, on a Ryzen 7 5700X (ParallelRecordWriteBenchmark): Write XLSX XLSB Serial 165.08 ms 113.61 ms Serial, PrefetchWrite 102.18 ms 62.39 ms Parallel, 1 batch in flight 164.23 ms 114.03 ms Parallel, 2 84.48 ms 58.53 ms Parallel, 4 44.27 ms 30.04 ms Parallel, 8 27.54 ms 19.48 ms Parallel, 16 21.64 ms 15.37 ms The file comes out 0.18% (XLSX) or 0.04% (XLSB) larger, because each batch is compressed on its own. As with PrefetchWrite, this is for single-file batch work: a server already writing many files at once has no idle cores to give it. From the native library and the bindings xl_write_typed and xl_write_typed_to_memory take the same two knobs in xl_write_options: degree_of_parallelism and batch_rows, with the same meaning (0 is every processor and the 8,192-row default). A zero-initialized struct therefore writes XLSX and XLSB in parallel; a struct with the 7.0 size (32 bytes) or a NULL options pointer writes serially, as before. The C++, Rust and Python wrappers default to a serial write and turn it on only when asked: xl::write_columns("big.xlsx", columns, {.degree_of_parallelism = 0}); write_columns("big.xlsx", &columns, &WriteOptions::new().degree_of_parallelism(0))?; write_workbook("big.xlsx", table, types, options=WriteOptions(degree_of_parallelism=0)) The table's buffers are read from several threads, so they must not change while the call runs. XLS, CSV and the xl_writer_handle API ignore both fields.
