python/README.html.title: excelreader (Python) | ExcelReader
python/README.html.summary: excelreader (Python) Read and write XLSX, XLSB, XLS and CSV through ExcelReader's NativeAOT library. No .NET runtime required — the shared library is self-contained. Install pip install excelreader-native Wheels ship for Windows x64, macOS (arm64, x64) and Linux (glibc and musl, x64 and arm64). The package installs as excelreader-native and imports as excelreader. Install (from source) python python/scripts/build_native.py # requires the .NET 10 SDK, once per machine pip install -e "python[dev]" build_native.py publishes src/ExcelReader.Native for your platform and copies the resulting ExcelReader.Native.{dll,so,dylib} into excelreader/_lib/. To point at a binary you built elsewhere, set EXCELREADER_NATIVE_LIB to its full path. Usage from excelreader import open_workbook with open_workbook("book.xlsx") as workbook: print(len(workbook.sheets), workbook.sheets[0].name) for row in workbook.sheets[0].rows(): for cell in row: print(cell.column, cell.type.name, cell.value) Sheets A workbook hands out sheets. workbook.sheets is a sequence: len(), iteration, and lookup by index (negative allowed), slice or name (names match without regard to case; a miss raises KeyError). A Sheet is the workbook and an index; it holds no native resource, and every read on it opens its own cursor. import excelreader with excelreader.open_workbook("report.xlsx") as workbook: for sheet in workbook.sheets: print(sheet.index, sheet.name, sheet.visibility) totals = workbook.sheets["Totals"] for row in totals.rows(): ... One open workbook can be read from several threads, which loads the shared-string table once. The native calls release the GIL: from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor with excelreader.open_workbook("report.xlsx") as workbook, ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool: tables = list(pool.map(lambda sheet: sheet.to_arrow(sheet.infer_schema()), workbook.sheets)) rows() and parse_batches() are generators: the native cursor opens at the first next(). A generator that has already started keeps working after workbook.close(); one that has not started raises at its first next(). to_arrow_stream() opens its stream at the call, so it works after close() even if never started. Tables workbook.tables lists the workbook's Excel tables ("Format as Table" ranges), with the same lookups as sheets: index, slice or name, ignoring case. A Table is a Sheet bounded to the table's range, so every read works on it and starts at the table's header row: with excelreader.open_workbook("report.xlsx") as workbook: sales = workbook.tables["Sales"] print(sales.name, sales.sheet.name, sales.first_row, sales.last_row) frame = sales.to_pandas(sales.infer_schema()) Rows and columns are zero-based and include the header and totals rows; cells keep the column indexes of the sheet holding the table. header_row_count is 0 for a table whose header row is turned off, and totals_row_count is 1 when it shows a totals row. A table is read on one thread whatever parallelism asks for. Formats open_workbook sniffs XLS/XLSX/XLSB by file signature. CSV has no signature, so it is chosen by the .csv extension — or explicitly: open_workbook("data.txt", format="csv") Dates cell.value is always the raw text as stored, so CellType.DATE cells hold Excel serial numbers. Use Cell.as_date() to convert, passing the workbook's epoch flag: as_date = cell.as_date(workbook.is_date1904) as_date() returns None for any cell that isn't CellType.DATE. Reading a sheet A sheet reads in one of these shapes: Method Returns Knob Needs rows() one list of Cell per row, streamed — nothing parse() the whole sheet as a TypedTable parallelism nothing parse_batches() one TypedTable per batch batch_size nothing to_arrow() the whole sheet as a pyarrow.RecordBatch parallelism pyarrow to_arrow_stream() an Arrow PyCapsule stream of batches batch_size nothing to_pandas() / to_polars() a DataFrame batch_size, parallelism pandas + pyarrow / polars infer_schema() guesses the schema every typed method takes. Typed columns — the fastest path rows() hands back cell text, which means the library formats every value to a string on the way out and builds one Python object per cell. parse() skips that entirely: you give it a schema, and the conversion happens natively, straight into typed column buffers. On a 65,536 × 14 sheet it is ~20× faster than rows(), and faster than polars.read_excel() — see Reading below for the measured numbers. from excelreader import ColumnSpec, ColumnType with open_workbook("sales.xlsb") as workbook: table = workbook.sheets[0].parse([ ColumnSpec(ColumnType.STRING, name="Region"), ColumnSpec(ColumnType.DATE, name="Order Date"), ColumnSpec(ColumnType.F64, name="Total Revenue", nullable=True), ]) table.row_count # rows read table.names # ["Region", "Order Date", "Total Revenue"] region, day, revenue = table.columns region[0] # "Asia" — strings decode on demand, not one str per row up front day[0] # 15477 — days since 1970-01-01 revenue[0] # 14862.69 table.validity[2] # bit-packed nulls, or None when the column has none Each non-string column is a stdlib array.array, or a NumPy array if NumPy is installed (pip install -e "python[numpy]") — NumPy is optional and never required. Leave name out to resolve a column by position instead: ColumnSpec(ColumnType.I64, index=3). header_row defaults to 1 (the first row names the columns); pass header_row=0 for a sheet with no header, where every spec must resolve by index. A column that fails to convert is an error unless its spec sets nullable=True, which records the failure in table.validity and keeps reading. parse() always reads the whole sheet from its first row, independent of any rows() generator in progress. Reading a sheet a batch at a time For a sheet too large to hold in memory at once, parse_batches() is parse() a batch at a time — a generator yielding one TypedTable per batch: with open_workbook("sales.xlsb") as workbook: schema = [ ColumnSpec(ColumnType.STRING, name="Region"), ColumnSpec(ColumnType.DATE, name="Order Date"), ColumnSpec(ColumnType.F64, name="Total Revenue", nullable=True), ] for batch in workbook.sheets[0].parse_batches(schema, batch_size=10_000): region, day, revenue = batch.columns ... batch_size is rows per batch; 0 means one unbounded batch, identical to parse(), and a negative value is an error. Chunked reads are independent: several can be open on one workbook at once, typed or Arrow (see Arrow below), and none disturbs another. Being a generator, parse_batches() opens nothing until the first iteration, so a bad batch_size is only raised there, not at the call. Reading a large sheet on several threads parse(), to_arrow(), to_pandas() and to_polars() take parallelism: 1 (the default) reads on one thread, 0 uses every core, n up to n threads. XLSX, XLSB and CSV are split. XLS, or a sheet under 256 KiB, is read on one thread with the same result. The table is identical either way. Every partition's columns are held until they are merged, so the peak memory is higher than a sequential read of the same file. to_pandas() and to_polars() with parallelism other than 1 parse the whole file instead of streaming it in batches. xl_parse_typed on a Ryzen 7 5700X (8 cores, 16 threads), 14 typed columns, file read from memory: File parallelism=1 parallelism=0 Speed-up 65K_Records_Data.csv (8 MB, 65,535 rows) 21.4 ms 5.8 ms 3.7x the same rows ×20 (160 MB, 1.3M rows) 425.9 ms 117.5 ms 3.6x The same call on the real-data workbooks (XLSX 6.7 MB compressed, XLSB 3.7 MB; measured with the published NativeAOT library): XLSX 54.1 ms at parallelism=1 against 20.3 ms at 0 (2.6x), XLSB 28.2 ms against 15.2 ms (1.85x). Inflate runs on one thread, so under the JIT the sheet stage stops scaling at about three threads. Peak working set on the 160 MB file, above the interpreter's own, went from 470 MiB to 503 MiB (both include the file's bytes and the handle's copy of them). Guessing a schema Writing the ColumnSpec list by hand means already knowing every column's name and type. When you don't, infer_schema() samples the sheet and guesses one for you: with open_workbook("sales.xlsb") as workbook: sheet = workbook.sheets[0] schema = sheet.infer_schema() # header_row=1, sample_size=100 by default table = sheet.parse(schema) By default each column's type comes from the CellType Excel already stored for its sampled cells, so it costs nothing beyond the sample and is exact for XLSX/XLSB/XLS. A column with a real mix of kinds, only formula/error results, or nothing sampled falls back to ColumnType.STRING; nullable is set when any sampled row left the column empty. CSV cells carry no such type tag, so by default every CSV column is guessed ColumnType.STRING. Pass parse_text=True to type text cells from their exact shape instead: integers, decimals, true/false and ISO dates or date-times. Codes with a leading zero (00123), scientific notation (12E4), padded or comma-decimal numbers and non-ISO dates stay strings. It is still a guess over the sample, so a value further down can fail to convert: with open_workbook("sales.csv") as workbook: sheet = workbook.sheets[0] schema = sheet.infer_schema(parse_text=True) table = sheet.parse(schema, parallelism=0) Writing write_workbook() writes a TypedTable (what parse() returns) back out as a single sheet, through the same xl_write_typed native export — one-shot, no writer handle before or after the call: from excelreader import ColumnType, write_workbook with open_workbook("sales.xlsb") as workbook: sheet = workbook.sheets[0] table = sheet.parse(sheet.infer_schema()) types = [ColumnType.STRING, ColumnType.DATE, ColumnType.F64] # one per table.columns, in order write_workbook("sales_copy.xlsx", table, types) types is required because a TypedTable column is a raw buffer (array/StringColumn/NumPy array) and nothing about the buffer alone tells I64 from TIME apart — both are 8-byte-per-row arrays. format is inferred from the path's extension (one of xlsx/xlsb/xls/csv) or set explicitly: write_workbook("report.dat", table, types, format="csv") The destination can also be a binary object with write(), such as io.BytesIO or an open file. The workbook is built in memory and written in one write() call, and with no extension to infer it from, format is required: import io buffer = io.BytesIO() write_workbook(buffer, table, types, format="xlsx") payload = buffer.getvalue() write_workbook() also takes Arrow-shaped data in place of a TypedTable: a pyarrow.RecordBatch or Table, a pandas DataFrame (its index is not written), or any table exposing __arrow_c_stream__, such as a polars DataFrame. Each column's type comes from its Arrow type, so leave types out. This path requires pyarrow: write_workbook("report.xlsx", df) # pandas write_workbook("report.xlsx", polars_df) # polars write_workbook("report.xlsx", record_batch) WriteOptions sets the sheet name and CSV dialect, mirroring xl_write_options — every field defaults to None, meaning "use the library default": from excelreader import WriteOptions write_workbook( "report.xlsx", table, types, options=WriteOptions(sheet_name="Q3 Results", use_shared_strings=True), ) For xlsx and xlsb, degree_of_parallelism formats and compresses batches of batch_rows rows on several threads: 0 uses every processor, 1 writes serially, and None is serial. A batch_rows of None keeps the library default of 8,192. With shared strings on, two parallel runs give the same content in files that differ byte for byte. xls and csv ignore both fields. write_workbook("big.xlsx", table, types, options=WriteOptions(degree_of_parallelism=0)) Phase-1 limits, stated plainly: write_workbook writes a single sheet (for several, see write_sheet below); the whole table must already be in memory (no streaming/chunked writes); no styling beyond the temporal number formats xl_write_typed applies to DATE/TIME/TIMESTAMP columns. format="auto" is not accepted — sniffing reads a file's existing signature bytes, and a file being created has none. Several sheets open_writer returns a SheetWriter, whose write_sheet writes a whole table as one sheet in a single native call. It takes the same data and types as write_workbook, so each sheet can be a TypedTable or a pandas, polars or pyarrow frame: from excelreader import WriteOptions, open_writer with open_writer("report.xlsx", options=WriteOptions(degree_of_parallelism=0)) as writer: writer.write_sheet("Sales", sales_df) writer.write_sheet("Stock", table, types) Parallelism and the other options come from open_writer and apply to every sheet; WriteOptions.sheet_name does not apply, since each call names its sheet. write_sheet raises ExcelReaderError while a sheet started with start_sheet is open; between sheets, the two styles mix freely. table=TableOptions(...) writes the sheet as an Excel table, with filter buttons and a table style (xlsx and xlsb only). The name must be unique in the workbook; the style defaults to TableStyleMedium2, and style=None leaves the table unstyled: from excelreader import TableOptions writer.write_sheet("Sales", sales_df, table=TableOptions("Sales", style="TableStyleLight9", column_stripes=True)) Writing a sheet row by row open_workbook's counterpart for writing one row at a time, instead of building a whole table first: import datetime from excelreader import open_writer with open_writer("out.xlsx") as writer: writer.start_sheet("Data") writer.write_row(["name", "qty", "when"]) writer.write_row(["widget", 7, datetime.date(2026, 1, 31)]) writer.end_sheet() Only a clean exit from the with block, or close(), commits the workbook. An exception inside the block, abort(), or a writer collected without being closed discards what was written and leaves an existing file at the path as it was. write_row picks each cell's type from the Python value: str, bool, int (64-bit), float, datetime.datetime (an aware one is converted to UTC), datetime.date and datetime.time. A None becomes a blank string cell; the tuple (None, ColumnType.I64) writes a blank cell of that type: writer.write_row(["widget", (None, ColumnType.I64), 2.5]) To build a workbook without touching the filesystem, open the writer over a binary object with write(), such as io.BytesIO. It needs format, and receives the finished workbook in one write() call when the writer closes: import io from excelreader import open_writer buffer = io.BytesIO() with open_writer(buffer, "xlsx") as writer: writer.start_sheet("Data") writer.write_row(["name", "qty"]) writer.end_sheet() payload = buffer.getvalue() Arrow With pyarrow installed, to_arrow() runs the same read and hands the buffers to pyarrow zero-copy over the Arrow C Data Interface, as one column-named pyarrow.RecordBatch: with open_workbook("sales.xlsb") as workbook: batch = workbook.sheets[0].to_arrow(schema) pyarrow owns the buffers from that point on, so the result stays valid after the workbook is closed. Streaming: Arrow streams, pandas, and polars to_arrow_stream() is to_arrow() a batch at a time — peak memory is one batch rather than one sheet. It returns a single-use stream implementing the Arrow PyCapsule interface (__arrow_c_stream__) and needs no third-party package itself; hand it to any consumer, such as pyarrow for a RecordBatchReader: import pyarrow as pa with open_workbook("sales.xlsb") as workbook: reader = pa.RecordBatchReader.from_stream(workbook.sheets[0].to_arrow_stream(schema, batch_size=10_000)) for batch in reader: frame = batch.to_pandas() # or polars.from_arrow(batch), for one DataFrame per batch Same batch_size rules as parse_batches() above, except to_arrow_stream() raises immediately rather than on the first iteration. The stream keeps working after the workbook is closed. to_pandas()/to_polars() materialize the whole sheet as a single DataFrame and both take batch_size and parallelism, but they spend batch_size differently — do not blur them. to_polars() genuinely streams: polars consumes the stream batch by batch, so the whole sheet is never resident as Arrow buffers at once. to_pandas() does not bound peak memory the same way — it concatenates every batch before pandas ever sees them. What batch_size buys to_pandas() instead is the conversion: self_destruct=True frees each Arrow chunk as pandas consumes it, so the sheet is never held twice, once as Arrow and once as the DataFrame. A faulted stream surfaces differently from every other native error in this library: pyarrow's RecordBatchReader reports a failed batch as a plain OSError carrying the native error message, not ExcelReaderError — the failure crosses the Arrow C Data Interface before this library's own exception wrapping ever runs. From memory, a stream, or your own bytes open_workbook() takes more than a path. bytes, bytearray, memoryview and io.BytesIO are read from memory; the format comes from the content, so pass format only for a CSV or to skip the check. with open_workbook(payload) as workbook: ... An object with a size and a read_at(offset, buffer) that fills buffer and returns the count is read in blocks on demand: the library asks for 4 MiB blocks and caches them, and every sheet can still be read on its own thread. import urllib.request from excelreader import open_workbook class HttpSource: def __init__(self, url): self.url = url with urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, method="HEAD")) as response: self.size = int(response.headers["Content-Length"]) def read_at(self, offset, buffer): request = urllib.request.Request(self.url, headers={"Range": f"bytes={offset}-{offset + len(buffer) - 1}"}) with urllib.request.urlopen(request) as response: data = response.read() buffer[: len(data)] = data return len(data) with open_workbook(HttpSource("https://example.com/book.xlsx")) as workbook: ... Any other object with readinto() or read(), such as an open file or sys.stdin.buffer, is read as a stream. A CSV is read as it arrives, and its first 16 MiB are kept so that infer_schema() followed by a read works; an XLSX, XLSB or XLS is read whole first. import sys from excelreader import open_workbook with open_workbook(sys.stdin.buffer, "csv") as workbook: ... Both callbacks run with the GIL held. For a file on disk, pass its path: that is faster. Reader options open_workbook() takes an optional OpenOptions for CSV dialect settings and reader resource limits. Every field defaults to None, meaning "use the library default", so you set only what you want to change. from excelreader import OpenOptions, open_workbook # A semicolon-delimited CSV, which the default comma dialect would read as one column per row. with open_workbook("export.csv", format="csv", options=OpenOptions(csv_delimiter=ord(";"))) as workbook: for row in workbook.sheets[0].rows(): ... csv_delimiter and csv_quote are byte values, so pass ord(";") rather than ";". max_cell_bytes and intern_strings apply to every format, a CSV included. The max_* fields are resource limits rather than tuning knobs: they bound what a malformed or hostile file can make the reader allocate, and exceeding one raises ExcelReaderError. Lower them when parsing untrusted uploads. options = OpenOptions( max_total_decompressed_bytes=64 * 1024 * 1024, # zip-bomb budget for XLSX/XLSB max_cell_bytes=1024 * 1024, max_zip_entries=1024, ) prefetch_decompression=True overlaps inflating an XLSX/XLSB sheet with parsing it — worth it for single-file batch work, not for a server already reading many files in parallel. See the root README for the measured trade. Each ZIP entry of an XLSX or XLSB is checked against its CRC-32 as it is read, so a damaged file raises ExcelReaderError instead of returning wrong cells. verify_zip_checksums=False turns the check off, for a file whose producer wrote wrong checksums. Encrypted workbooks open_workbook() takes a password keyword to open a password-protected OOXML workbook (.xlsx/.xlsb/.xlsm): from excelreader import PasswordIncorrectError, open_workbook try: with open_workbook("protected.xlsx", password="hunter2") as workbook: ... except PasswordIncorrectError: ... # ask again Omitting password for an encrypted file raises PasswordRequiredError; a wrong one raises PasswordIncorrectError — both subclass ExcelReaderError, so a caller that doesn't care about the distinction can just catch that. Any other native failure (an unsupported encryption scheme, a corrupt file) also raises ExcelReaderError but is not worth retrying. An explicit format="xlsx"/format="xlsb" works for an encrypted file too, the same as leaving format unset — both routes decrypt correctly given the right password. Writing an encrypted workbook is a second step: write the plaintext package with write_workbook or open_writer, then wrap it with encrypt_package, which produces an agile-encrypted (ECMA-376 4.4) CFB container — AES-256-CBC, SHA-512, 100,000 spin iterations, with a dataIntegrity HMAC: from excelreader import encrypt_package, write_workbook write_workbook("plain.xlsx", table, types) encrypt_package("plain.xlsx", "secret.xlsx", "hunter2") The package must already be a finished file; it is read, not removed. Encryption parameters are fixed at Excel's own defaults — there are no options — and only XLSX/XLSB packages can be encrypted, matching what open_workbook can decrypt. Either side can stay in memory, so the plaintext package never has to be written to disk: the package can be bytes or an io.BytesIO, and the destination any binary object with write(): import io from excelreader import encrypt_package, write_workbook plain, secret = io.BytesIO(), io.BytesIO() write_workbook(plain, table, types, format="xlsx") encrypt_package(plain, secret, "hunter2") Benchmarks benchmarks/bench_read.py and benchmarks/bench_write.py over tests/ExcelReader.Benchmarks/Data/65K_Records_Data.xlsb (65,535 data rows, 14 columns), the same fixture the .NET, C++ and Rust suites use. Measured on Windows 10 (22H2), AMD Ryzen 7 5700X (16 logical CPUs @ 3.39 GHz), CPython 3.14.7, 10 runs each (medians shown; min is in the scripts' own output), against a library published from commit ef831b19. Competitors: polars 2.0.0 (with fastexcel 0.21.0), pandas 3.1.0 (with openpyxl 3.1.5), xlsxwriter 3.2.9. Reading API Median What it produces to_arrow() 31.2 ms the same parse, handed to pyarrow zero-copy to_arrow_stream(), read by pyarrow 32.0 ms Arrow record batches, streamed parse() 33.8 ms typed columnar buffers, converted natively parse_batches() 34.9 ms the same typed buffers, in batches to_polars() 35.4 ms typed columnar DataFrame, schema inferred polars.read_excel() 135.0 ms typed columnar DataFrame, types inferred rows() 693.8 ms one Cell object per cell, streamed per row The batched readers cost the same as their whole-sheet counterparts and lower the peak memory: to_arrow_stream(batch_size=10000) peaks at 10.9 MiB against 19.4 MiB for one whole-sheet record batch on this file. Only the to_polars() / polars.read_excel() pair is a like-for-like comparison (~3.8x), and even that one is loose: both produce a typed columnar DataFrame with inferred types, but the inference rules are not identical. The rows above it produce different things and are listed to show what each API costs, not to rank them — rows() is ~20x slower than parse() because it materializes 917,504 Python objects, which is the price of that shape, not a slow parser. CSV, from 65K_Records_Data.csv (8.2 MB), same 14 typed columns: API Median parse(parallelism=1) 25.8 ms parse(parallelism=0) 13.7 ms to_polars(parallelism=1) 25.3 ms to_polars(parallelism=0) 11.3 ms polars.read_csv(try_parse_dates=True) 12.9 ms pandas.read_csv, pyarrow engine 114.5 ms pandas.read_csv, C engine 73.0 ms At parallelism=0 ExcelReader and polars' multithreaded CSV reader are level (to_polars() 11.3 ms against 12.9 ms; polars infers types from the text, we convert against a given schema). ExcelReader is ~5x faster than pandas' C engine and ~8x faster than its pyarrow engine, measured with parse(parallelism=0). These include opening the file, so they are above the in-memory xl_parse_typed figures in Reading a large sheet on several threads. Writing API Median Output write_workbook() → csv 35.9 ms 8.2 MB write_workbook() → xls 53.0 ms 13.4 MB write_workbook() → xlsb 53.7 ms 4.5 MB write_workbook() → xlsx 68.8 ms 5.1 MB write_workbook(polars_df) → xlsx 76.1 ms 5.1 MB write_workbook(pandas_df) → xlsx 82.4 ms 5.1 MB polars.DataFrame.write_excel() 4,754.8 ms 5.6 MB pandas.DataFrame.to_excel() 7,696.4 ms 5.5 MB The two DataFrame comparisons are matched work — same DataFrame in, xlsx out both times: write_workbook(polars_df) is ~62x faster than polars' own write_excel(), and write_workbook(pandas_df) ~93x faster than to_excel(). Both of ours pay a conversion the raw path does not: the DataFrame goes through Arrow, and each column is cast to the layout the native side reads and copied out of Arrow's buffers, which is the gap between those rows and the 68.8 ms one. Handing write_workbook() buffers that are already columnar — what parse() returns — skips it. write_workbook(xlsx) at 68.8 ms lands within ~3 ms of the C++ binding's xl::write_columns on the same 14 columns (65.7 ms), which is the expected result: both are thin wrappers over the same xl_write_typed call, and neither adds work per cell. xls being the largest file and still faster than xlsx is not a paradox — BIFF8 writes fixed-width records with no compression, so it trades ~2.6x the bytes for less work per cell. xlsb costs about the same, at 53.7 ms. Notes A Workbook can be read from several threads at once; see Sheets. Empty cells are skipped, so cell.column may skip indices. Do not assume row[i].column == i. The ABI is documented in src/ExcelReader.Native/include/excelreader.h.

rust/excelreader/README.html.title: excelreader (Rust) | ExcelReader
rust/excelreader/README.html.summary: excelreader (Rust) Read and write Excel/CSV workbooks via ExcelReader's native ABI: opening a workbook (from a path, memory, your own random-access source or any Read), sheet navigation, schema inference, schema-driven typed parse, schema-driven writing, row-by-row reads, parallel CSV aggregation, and Arrow export. Every public item lives at the crate root. Usage [dependencies] excelreader = "7.0" use excelreader::{ExcelMapper, Workbook, ReadOptions}; #[derive(Default, ExcelMapper)] struct Row { #[excel(name = "Name")] name: String, #[excel(name = "Count")] count: u32, } let workbook = Workbook::open("book.xlsx")?; let table = workbook.sheet(0)?.parse::<Row>(&ReadOptions::new())?; for row in table.iter() { /* ... */ } # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Sheet::parse(header_row, degree_of_parallelism) converts on the native side and never formats a cell to text, so it is the fastest way to read a sheet whose columns you know. header_row is 1-based (0 = no header); degree_of_parallelism is 0 for every processor, 1 sequential, n up to n threads - XLSX, XLSB and CSV are split, and the table is the same whatever it is. Field types Field type Column String ColumnType::String i8..i64, isize, u8..u64, usize ColumnType::I64 f32, f64 ColumnType::F64 bool ColumnType::Bool Date / chrono::NaiveDate ColumnType::Date Time / chrono::NaiveTime ColumnType::Time Timestamp / chrono::NaiveDateTime ColumnType::Timestamp Option<T> of any of the above makes the field None when the cell is null; a non-Option field is left at its Default instead. Narrower integers convert through TryFrom and panic on a value that does not fit, rather than wrapping silently. Date/Time/Timestamp are dependency-free newtypes over the exact wire representation; enable the chrono feature to use chrono's calendar types directly: excelreader = { version = "7.0", features = ["chrono"] } Opening Workbook::open(path) sniffs the format and uses every library default. Everything else goes through OpenOptions, in the style of std::fs::OpenOptions: set what you need, then call open, open_bytes, open_source or open_reader. use excelreader::{Format, OpenOptions}; let options = OpenOptions::new().format(Format::Csv).csv_delimiter(b';' as i32); let from_path = options.open("data.csv")?; let from_memory = options.open_bytes(b"a;b\n1;2\n")?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Format sniffing (Format::Auto, the default) does not detect CSV - set Format::Csv. The resource limits (max_total_decompressed_bytes, max_cell_bytes, max_shared_string_bytes, max_zip_entries, max_buffered_bytes) protect against hostile files; lower them when opening untrusted input. Sheets and schema inference A workbook hands out sheets. A Sheet is the workbook and an index: it holds no native resource, it is Copy, and every read on it opens its own cursor. # use excelreader::Workbook; let workbook = Workbook::open("report.xlsx")?; for sheet in workbook.sheets()? { println!("{} {:?}", sheet.name()?, sheet.visibility()?); } // Guess a schema from the header row plus a sample of the data, before committing to one. let sheet = workbook.sheet_by_name("Totals")?.expect("the workbook has a Totals sheet"); for column in sheet.infer_schema(1, 100, false)? { println!("{:?} -> {:?}", column.name, column.column_type); } # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) infer_schema's last argument, parse_text, also types text cells (every CSV field, or numbers stored as text): integers, decimals, true/false and ISO dates. With no row type, parse_with_schema reads the sheet through that schema into a Table. Its columns are the Columns write_columns takes, so the table writes back as it was read: use excelreader::{write_columns, ColumnData, ReadOptions, Workbook, WriteOptions}; let workbook = Workbook::open("book.xlsx")?; let sheet = workbook.sheet(0)?; let schema = sheet.infer_schema(1, 100, false)?; let table = sheet.parse_with_schema(&schema, &ReadOptions::new())?; for column in table.columns() { if let ColumnData::I64(values) = column.data { println!("{:?}: {} integers", column.name, values.len()); } } write_columns("copy.xlsx", &table.columns(), &WriteOptions::new())?; // Or a batch at a time: TableBatches yields one Table per batch. for batch in sheet.parse_batches_with_schema(&schema, &ReadOptions::new())? { println!("{} rows", batch?.len()); } # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) A column matched by index has no name, and writing needs every column named or none. The schema is a guess over a sample: a column inferred as I64 that holds a fraction further down fails the read, unless the column is nullable. Workbook is Send + Sync, so sheets can be read in parallel over one open workbook, which loads the shared-string table once: # use excelreader::Workbook; # let workbook = Workbook::open("report.xlsx")?; let tables = std::thread::scope(|scope| { let handles: Vec<_> = workbook .sheets()? .into_iter() .map(|sheet| scope.spawn(move || sheet.read_all())) .collect(); handles.into_iter().map(|handle| handle.join().expect("no panic")).collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>() })?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Tables Workbook::tables lists the workbook's Excel tables ("Format as Table" ranges) as TableInfo: name, the sheet holding it, and its zero-based range, header and totals rows included. Workbook::table(index) and table_by_name(name) (ignoring case) return a Sheet bounded to the table, so every read works on it and starts at the table's header row: # use excelreader::{ReadOptions, Workbook}; # #[derive(Default, excelreader::ExcelMapper)] # struct Sale { #[excel(name = "Units")] units: i64 } let workbook = Workbook::open("report.xlsx")?; for table in workbook.tables()? { println!("{} on sheet {}: rows {}..={}", table.name, table.sheet, table.first_row, table.last_row); } if let Some(sales) = workbook.table_by_name("Sales")? { let rows = sales.parse::<Sale>(&ReadOptions::new())?; println!("{} sales", rows.len()); } # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Cells keep the column indexes of the sheet holding the table, and the table's Sheet::name is that sheet's. A table is read on one thread whatever the degree of parallelism asks for. Encrypted workbooks OpenOptions::password unlocks a password-protected OOXML workbook (.xlsx/.xlsb/.xlsm): use excelreader::{ErrorKind, OpenOptions}; match OpenOptions::new().password("hunter2").open("protected.xlsx") { Ok(workbook) => { /* ... */ } Err(e) if e.kind() == ErrorKind::PasswordIncorrect => { /* ask again */ } Err(e) if e.kind() == ErrorKind::PasswordRequired => { /* no password was supplied */ } Err(other) => { /* unsupported scheme or a corrupt file; not worth retrying */ } } Every Error carries an ErrorKind to branch on and the native detail in message(). Format sniffing does not see through the CFB wrapper an encrypted file is stored in, so keep the default Format::Auto rather than setting Format::Xlsx, or the file is read as a plain ZIP and fails before the password is ever checked. Writing an encrypted workbook is a second step: write the plaintext package with write_columns/ write_sheet, then wrap it with encrypt_package, which produces an agile-encrypted (ECMA-376 4.4) CFB container - AES-256-CBC, SHA-512, 100,000 spin iterations, with a dataIntegrity HMAC: use excelreader::{encrypt_package, write_columns, WriteOptions}; # use excelreader::{Column, ColumnData}; # let ids = [1i64, 2, 3]; # let columns = [Column::new(Some("id"), ColumnData::I64(&ids))]; write_columns("plain.xlsx", &columns, &WriteOptions::new())?; encrypt_package("plain.xlsx", "secret.xlsx", "hunter2")?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) package_path is read twice (it is not disposed or removed), so it must already be a finished file. Encryption parameters are fixed at Excel's own defaults - there are no options - and only XLSX/XLSB packages can be encrypted, matching what OpenOptions::password can decrypt. Reading from your own bytes Implement [Source] to read from anything you can read at an offset. The library calls read_at from several threads, fetching 4 MiB blocks it caches; every sheet can still be read in parallel. struct HttpSource { client: reqwest::blocking::Client, url: String, size: u64 } impl excelreader::Source for HttpSource { fn size(&self) -> std::io::Result<u64> { Ok(self.size) } fn read_at(&self, offset: u64, buf: &mut [u8]) -> std::io::Result<usize> { let range = format!("bytes={}-{}", offset, offset + buf.len() as u64 - 1); let bytes = self.client.get(&self.url).header("Range", range).send() .and_then(|r| r.error_for_status()) .and_then(|r| r.bytes()) .map_err(std::io::Error::other)?; buf[..bytes.len()].copy_from_slice(&bytes); Ok(bytes.len()) } } let workbook = OpenOptions::new().open_source(source)?; Anything that implements Read works through open_reader. A CSV is read as it arrives; an XLSX, XLSB or XLS is read whole first. # use excelreader::{Format, OpenOptions}; let workbook = OpenOptions::new().format(Format::Csv).open_reader(std::io::stdin())?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) An io::Error from your source, or a panic in it, comes back as the Error of the call that needed the bytes. Arrow export (arrow feature) excelreader = { version = "7.0", features = ["arrow"] } # #[cfg(feature = "arrow")] # fn main() -> Result<(), excelreader::Error> { use excelreader::{Workbook, ReadOptions}; # #[derive(Default, excelreader::ExcelMapper)] # struct Row { #[excel(name = "Name")] name: String } let workbook = Workbook::open("book.xlsx")?; let batch = workbook.sheet(0)?.to_arrow::<Row>(&ReadOptions::new())?; println!("{} rows x {} columns", batch.num_rows(), batch.num_columns()); # Ok(()) # } # #[cfg(not(feature = "arrow"))] # fn main() {} Off by default — arrow-rs is a large dependency and the typed-parse path needs none of it. Batched: Sheet::to_arrow_stream is parse_arrow delivered a batch at a time, returning ArrowBatches<'_>, an Iterator<Item = Result<RecordBatch, ArrowError>> that also implements RecordBatchReader: # #[cfg(feature = "arrow")] # fn main() -> Result<(), excelreader::Error> { use excelreader::{Workbook, ReadOptions}; # #[derive(Default, excelreader::ExcelMapper)] # struct Row { #[excel(name = "Name")] name: String } let workbook = Workbook::open("book.xlsx")?; let mut chunks = workbook.sheet(0)?.to_arrow_stream::<Row>(&ReadOptions::new())?; while let Some(batch) = chunks.next() { let Ok(batch) = batch else { break }; // ArrowBatches does not fuse, unlike TypedBatches println!("{} rows", batch.num_rows()); } # Ok(()) # } # #[cfg(not(feature = "arrow"))] # fn main() {} Same batch_size semantics as parse_batches below. Unlike TypedBatches, ArrowBatches does not fuse after an error — it follows arrow-rs's own semantics — so break on the first Err rather than continuing the loop. With no row type, to_arrow_with_schema and to_arrow_stream_with_schema take the columns at run time instead, such as the ones infer_schema returned. A column with a name is matched by it, one without by its index: # #[cfg(feature = "arrow")] # fn main() -> Result<(), excelreader::Error> { use excelreader::{Workbook, ReadOptions}; let workbook = Workbook::open("book.xlsx")?; let sheet = workbook.sheet(0)?; let schema = sheet.infer_schema(1, 100, false)?; let batch = sheet.to_arrow_with_schema(&schema, &ReadOptions::new())?; # Ok(()) # } # #[cfg(not(feature = "arrow"))] # fn main() {} The schema is a guess over a sample: a column inferred as I64 that holds a fraction further down fails the read, unless the column is nullable. Writing #[derive(ExcelMapper)] generates both halves, so the same struct reads and writes - the field types in the table above apply unchanged: use excelreader::{write_sheet, WriteOptions}; # #[derive(Default, excelreader::ExcelMapper)] # struct Row { #[excel(name = "Name")] name: String } # let rows = vec![Row::default()]; write_sheet("out.xlsx", &rows, &WriteOptions::new())?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Option<T> fields become an LSB-first validity bitmap: None writes a blank cell rather than a zero. Only the primary #[excel(name = "...")] reaches the header - the alias list exists to resolve a header on the way in, and the ABI rejects a write column carrying more than one name. For buffers that are already columnar, write_columns borrows them and copies nothing. The lifetimes on Column<'a> are what turn the ABI's borrow contract into something the compiler checks: use excelreader::{write_columns, Column, ColumnData, WriteOptions}; let ids = [1i64, 2, 3]; let columns = [Column::new(Some("id"), ColumnData::I64(&ids))]; write_columns("out.xlsx", &columns, &WriteOptions::new())?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) validity is checked against the row count before the call: the ABI takes the bitmap without a length and reads (rows + 7) / 8 bytes on trust, so a short slice would be a buffer overrun rather than a wrong answer. WriteOptions sets the format, the sheet name, the CSV dialect, and the XLS/XLSB and XLSX/XLSB toggles. Its format defaults to Format::Auto, inferred from the path's extension; an extension it does not recognize is an error - a file being created has no signature bytes to sniff. For XLSX and XLSB, degree_of_parallelism formats and compresses batches of batch_rows rows on several threads: 0 uses every processor, 1 writes serially, and leaving it unset is serial. Unset batch_rows keeps the library default of 8,192. With shared strings on, two parallel runs give the same content in files that differ byte for byte. XLS, CSV and WriterHandle's per-cell writes ignore both. use excelreader::{write_columns, Column, ColumnData, WriteOptions}; # let ids = [1i64, 2, 3]; # let columns = [Column::new(Some("id"), ColumnData::I64(&ids))]; write_columns("big.xlsx", &columns, &WriteOptions::new().degree_of_parallelism(0))?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Each write has a path form and an io::Write form: write_columns_to/write_sheet_to build the workbook in memory and write it to the writer in one write_all. A writer has no extension, so these need an explicit format: use excelreader::{write_sheet_to, Format, WriteOptions}; # #[derive(Default, excelreader::ExcelMapper)] # struct Row { #[excel(name = "Name")] name: String } # let rows = vec![Row::default()]; let mut bytes = Vec::new(); write_sheet_to(&mut bytes, &rows, &WriteOptions::new().format(Format::Xlsx))?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) write_sheet walks the slice once and appends each field to its own buffer, monomorphized per field. That transpose is the only copy it makes; write_columns pays nothing. Streaming writes write_sheet/write_columns build the whole table in memory first. WriterHandle is the row-by-row alternative, writing directly as each call arrives instead: use excelreader::{WriteOptions, WriterHandle}; let mut handle = WriterHandle::create("out.xlsx", &WriteOptions::new())?; handle.start_sheet("Summary")?; handle.start_row()?; handle.write_str(Some("Name"))?; handle.write_i64(Some(42))?; handle.end_row()?; handle.end_sheet()?; handle.finish()?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Call order mirrors the C ABI's xl_writer_handle: create (a path) or new (any io::Write), then per sheet start_sheet..end_sheet, each containing start_row..end_row with one write_* call per cell (None writes a blank cell), left to right, then finish. A call out of order returns Err rather than corrupting output. A handle from new writes the whole workbook to its writer once, in finish. Only finish commits: dropping a handle without finishing it (an early ? return, a panic) discards what was written, leaves an existing file at the path as it was, and writes nothing to a writer. To write several sheets from whole tables, call the handle's write_sheet or write_columns once per sheet. They take what the free functions take, plus the sheet's name, and write it in one call instead of one per cell, using the handle's degree_of_parallelism and batch_rows. Between sheets they mix with start_sheet..end_sheet; while a sheet is open they return Err. use excelreader::{WriteOptions, WriterHandle}; # #[derive(Default, excelreader::ExcelMapper)] # struct Row { #[excel(name = "Name")] name: String } # let sales = vec![Row::default()]; # let stock = vec![Row::default()]; let mut handle = WriterHandle::create("report.xlsx", &WriteOptions::new().degree_of_parallelism(0))?; handle.write_sheet("Sales", &sales, None)?; handle.write_sheet("Stock", &stock, None)?; handle.finish()?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Passing Some(&TableOptions::new("Sales")) writes the sheet as an Excel table, with filter buttons and a table style (XLSX and XLSB only, every column named). The name must be unique in the workbook; the style defaults to TableStyleMedium2, and .style(None) leaves the table unstyled. Reading rows one at a time Sheet::rows returns a cursor over that sheet. Each row borrows a buffer the cursor reuses, so iterating a sheet allocates nothing per row: use excelreader::Workbook; let workbook = Workbook::open("book.xlsx")?; let mut cursor = workbook.sheet(0)?.rows()?; while let Some(row) = cursor.next_row() { let row = row?; for cell in row.iter() { print!("{}\t", cell.as_str()?); } println!(); } # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Because each row borrows the cursor's buffer, only one row is alive at a time — the borrow checker enforces it. To hold every row at once, use read_all, which reads the whole sheet in one native call into one buffer and keeps it alive until dropped: # use excelreader::Workbook; let workbook = Workbook::open("book.xlsx")?; let rows = workbook.sheet(0)?.read_all()?; for row in rows.iter() { println!("{} cells", row.len()); } # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Chunked reads For a sheet too large to hold in memory at once, Sheet::parse_batches is Sheet::parse delivered a batch at a time: use excelreader::{Workbook, ReadOptions}; # #[derive(Default, excelreader::ExcelMapper)] # struct Row { #[excel(name = "Name")] name: String } let workbook = Workbook::open("book.xlsx")?; let chunks = workbook.sheet(0)?.parse_batches::<Row>(&ReadOptions::new())?; for batch in chunks { let batch = batch?; for row in batch.iter() { /* ... */ } } # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) parse_batches returns TypedBatches<'_, Row>, an Iterator<Item = Result<TableView<Row>, Error>> that closes the native reader on drop. batch_size is rows per batch — 0 means one unbounded batch, identical to parse; negative is an error. Chunked reads, of either kind (typed or Arrow — see Arrow export above), are independent: several can be live on one workbook, and other reads do not disturb them. TypedBatches ends after yielding an Err, so a for loop stops there rather than spinning on it. Parallel CSV aggregation aggregate_csv folds a CSV file or buffer into one accumulator across several threads, without building a table. The CSV dialect and cell limit come from OpenOptions: use excelreader::{aggregate_csv, CsvAccumulator, OpenOptions, RowRef}; struct Count(u64); impl CsvAccumulator for Count { fn accumulate(&mut self, _row: RowRef<'_>) -> Result<(), i32> { self.0 += 1; Ok(()) } fn combine(&mut self, other: &mut Self) -> Result<(), i32> { self.0 += other.0; Ok(()) } } let options = OpenOptions::new().csv_delimiter(b';' as i32); let rows = aggregate_csv("big.csv", &options, 1, 0, || Count(0))?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) The input is a path (&str, &Path, &PathBuf) or bytes (&[u8]); then header_row and degree_of_parallelism, as in Sheet::parse. A nonzero code from a callback comes back as ErrorKind::Callback(code); a panic in one is resumed on the calling thread. Callback reads Sheet::for_each_row calls a closure once per row on the calling thread, with cells borrowed from the library's buffers for that call instead of copied into a cursor: use excelreader::Workbook; let workbook = Workbook::open("report.xlsx")?; let mut total = 0.0; workbook.sheet(0)?.for_each_row(|row| { if let Some(amount) = row.get(1).and_then(|cell| cell.number()) { total += amount; } Ok(()) })?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) Sheet::aggregate folds any sheet, in any format, into one accumulator across several threads. New code should use it rather than aggregate_csv: use excelreader::{Accumulator, RowRef, Workbook}; struct Count(u64); impl Accumulator for Count { fn accumulate(&mut self, _row: RowRef<'_>) -> Result<(), i32> { self.0 += 1; Ok(()) } fn combine(&mut self, other: &mut Self) -> Result<(), i32> { self.0 += other.0; Ok(()) } } let workbook = Workbook::open("big.xlsx")?; let rows = workbook.sheet(0)?.aggregate(1, 0, || Count(0))?; # Ok::<(), excelreader::Error>(()) A cell in these callbacks carries text, a number, or both. as_bytes/as_str return only the stored text, so they are empty for a cell that carries only a number; text() formats that number itself (shortest round-trip form) and number() returns it directly, or parses the text when there is no number. A positive Err(code) comes back as ErrorKind::Callback(code), and a panic is resumed on the calling thread. Calling other methods on the workbook from inside the callback is allowed. Sheet::aggregate seeds an accumulator per chunk of sheet data, not per thread, and may drop a chunk's accumulator without combining it. XLS, table views and CSV opened from a Source or stream read sequentially. Bounds and panics TableView::get returns Option<T> and is None outside 0..len(). The accessors the derive's generated code reads columns through panic on an out-of-range row, a column type that does not match the binding, or a string the native library returned as non-UTF-8 - each is a contract violation rather than recoverable input. Build notes build.rs downloads the native ExcelReader.Native binary matching your target from the crate's matching GitHub Release. Set EXCELREADER_NATIVE_LIB_DIR to a directory containing a locally-built copy instead (e.g. from dotnet publish ../../src/ExcelReader.Native -r win-x64) to skip that download - useful when building from source before a release exists yet. Every constructor first checks the loaded library's ABI revision against the one this crate was compiled against, and fails with an explanatory error rather than reading native memory through a layout that may have changed. Benchmarks Criterion suite in benches/. Measured on Windows 10 (22H2), 16 logical CPUs @ 3.39 GHz, rustc 1.97.1 (Release), Criterion 0.8, 100 samples per benchmark (medians shown). write_bench takes 20 samples instead — each of its iterations writes a whole 65,535-row file. benches/parse_bench.rs - open/Sheet::parse/infer_schema, same methodology as the C++ suite: Benchmark RealExcel.xlsb (100 rows) 65K_Records_Data.xlsb (65,535 rows) open 90.5 µs 102.1 µs parse_sheet (2 or 6 bound columns) 57.9 µs 24.9 ms typed chunks of 1,000 / 10,000 rows - 23.4 ms / 23.4 ms infer_schema (sample 100 / 1,000 rows) 89.7 µs 611.1 µs open stays nearly flat across the 655x row-count jump (+13%) - XLSB's header carries its dimensions/index, so opening costs metadata, not row data. parse_sheet scales linearly with rows × columns. Reading the same sheet in typed chunks costs no more than one whole-sheet parse_sheet, while holding only one chunk at a time. infer_schema scales with its sample size, not the file's total row count. benches/compare_bench.rs compares against calamine reading 65K_Records_Data.{xlsx,xlsb} in full (all 14 columns, 65,535 rows). Both sides decode every cell into an owned value (String for text) and fold it into one accumulator, so neither side gets a zero-copy advantage the other can't take: Format ExcelReader (Sheet::parse::<FullRow>) calamine (worksheet_range + Data match) XLSX 69.5 ms 276.4 ms XLSB 47.8 ms 87.0 ms ExcelReader is ~4.0x faster than calamine for XLSX and ~1.8x faster for XLSB on this workload - calamine is a fast, well-optimized reader in its own right, so the gap is real but not the order of magnitude seen against slower libraries. benches/write_bench.rs measures the two write layers and rust_xlsxwriter writing the same 7 columns × 65,535 rows to .xlsx, all three starting from the same in-memory Vec<Row>: Benchmark Median columns (write_columns, pre-transposed) 35.0 ms sheet (write_sheet, from Vec<Row>) 40.8 ms rust_xlsxwriter (cell-at-a-time) 338.5 ms sheet is the matched-work number — it starts from the same shape rust_xlsxwriter is handed and pays the row-to-column transpose itself — and is ~8.3x faster. columns is a ceiling no cell-at-a-time API can reach, since it is handed buffers that are already columnar; read it only against sheet, as the cost of having row-shaped data in the first place. That cost turns out to be about 17%: not free, but a minority of the cost of producing the file. Two caveats, both running against the headline number rather than for it. ExcelReader does slightly more work here: it attaches a number format to the date column so Excel shows a date, and writes a header row, while the rust_xlsxwriter case writes that column as a bare serial number and no header. And rust_xlsxwriter carries formatting and formula support this library does not expose at all, so its number reflects a different feature set, not only a slower path. Run locally: cd rust EXCELREADER_NATIVE_LIB_DIR=/path/to/native/lib/dir cargo bench -p excelreader EXCELREADER_NATIVE_LIB_DIR should point at a directory containing a locally-built ExcelReader.Native.{dll,so,dylib} - see Build notes above. Pass --bench parse_bench, --bench compare_bench or --bench write_bench to run one suite only.
